The Retiree's Portfolio

follows a retiree who puts $1 million into Vanguard funds and draws an income that rises every year, from every start year since 1995, not one lucky one: holding cash or bonds alone, the S&P 500, a plain two-fund index mix, and choosing the best-ranked funds — picked once and kept, re-ranked within the list of the first day of retirement, or from the whole menu each January. It looks first at how low the money fell on the way, then at what was left. Before the funds, it follows the same retirement over market history back to 1872.

title: The answer in brief
subtitle: A retiree puts $1 million into Vanguard funds and draws a rising income: what was left, and how low it fell, for every start year since 1995

, the preface and the answer in brief —

Start here
Preface

This book examines a single question across thirty years of market history. How does a retirement fare when the retiree holds whichever Vanguard funds have performed best recently, re-selecting them each January, while drawing a fixed and rising income? And does it fare better than holding the market through two index funds and never choosing at all?
History, not a forecast.

This book is a record of the past: how cash, bonds, the S&P 500, their mixes and a few ways of choosing funds behaved in the retirements that actually happened, over periods of ten to fifty years. Each retirement is one history — anecdotal evidence, not a probability. Nothing in the book says which funds or which mix will do best in the years ahead, none of it is a recommendation to buy or hold any fund, and no future selection is offered anywhere in it. The book repeats this wherever it turns to a new part of the record.

The question is asked not of one retirement but of every year in which a retirement could have begun since 1995. The same withdrawal rule is then run over the long market histories, from 1872, to reach the start years the study's own thirty years cannot: the crash of 1929 and the inflation that followed the mid-1960s.
A credible answer depends on details that are easy to get wrong and difficult to detect once they are wrong:
which funds were genuinely available
on the day a choice was made;
which were closed
to new investors;
which later merged or were liquidated
how each fund's early price history
was recorded;
when withdrawals are taken
where the money is held
until it is spent.
Each of these details altered the answer at some stage of the work, and several reversed it. The study proceeded through a sequence of numbered tests, each listed in
appendix B
, and a series of documented corrections.

The book has nine parts, in the order a portfolio is built. Part I sets the question. Part II asks what safe money alone can do — cash, then bonds; Part III what the S&P 500 adds; Part IV how a mix of the two behaves, over the study's years and over the long market histories, and whether moving the split from year to year helps. Part V sets out the method of choosing funds, Part VI the results, Part VII a different way of drawing the income — a cash bucket holding two years of withdrawals — and Part VIII what the results support and the errors corrected along the way. Part IX turns back to the years of saving that come before retirement. "How to read this book" describes each part.

It is written for readers who wish to understand what the figures mean and how far they can be relied upon, not only what they are. The answer in brief, which follows, gives the result at once; the rest of the book shows how it was reached, one piece at a time, and how far it holds.
The answer in brief

Which matters more to a retiree: the most money at the end, or the highest lowest point along the way — the point at which a retiree might have given up on the plan or gone back to work? This summary gives both, and its comparisons take the lowest point first.
The setting: a retiree starting in any year from 1995 to 2006 with $1 million, 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, following the withdrawal rule of
chapter 1

for twenty years. Both measures are shown as the median and the worst of the 12 retirements. Beside each worst low point, "N yr M mo in" is how far into that retirement it fell, counted in calendar months from January of the start year (see "Terms used throughout" below).
History, not a forecast.

Every result in this book is an observed historical retirement — what happened to a particular retiree in particular years, not an estimate of what will happen to the next one. The only exceptions say so where they appear:
chapter 24

and appendix G.9 carry a few balances past the last data date at an assumed constant return, as an illustration. Nothing else is projected or simulated. How many complete retirements exist depends on the length and on the data:

How often a retirement ran out over thirty, forty or fifty years is known only for the long histories
(chapters 10 to 12) — for mixes of the S&P 500 and bonds and for the rule of
chapter 12

The menu each January held a higher floor than the plain index, and ended lower.

Its worst low point was $515k against the plain index's $492k (both the 2000 retirement, in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), its median low point $755k against $674k, and its low point was the higher in 9 of 12 retirements. mostly long-term bond funds, not from its stock picks, and that bond bet reversed in 2022 (

Its worst low point, $476k (the 2000 retirement, 9 yr 2 mo in), was below the plain index's $492k and the menu's $515k; its median low point, $721k, was above the plain index's $674k, though below the menu's $755k; and at 60/40 and 50/50 its worst low point was above the plain index's, though still below the menu's. 70/30 is one sample, not a recommendation.

Were the study's twelve retirements the hardest a retiree could have met? The long market histories say not;
chapter 12
then tests a rule that moves the split.
The long histories.

With fixed mixes of the S&P 500 and a 10-year Treasury, the hardest twenty-year retirements at 70/30 under the study's rule began in 1928, 1929 and 1930, and 1 of 79 ran out; with withdrawals rising with inflation, the hardest thirty-year retirements began in 1965 and 1966.
The hard stop over the study's twelve retirements.
Chapter 12

moves the split each January, and to 20% stocks and 80% bonds whenever the S&P 500 is 20% below its high. On the two index funds day by day, that hard stop held a far higher floor than the plain index at 70/30 (as Part VI simulates it, with its Treasury-bill account): a worst low point of $755k against $492k (both the 2000 retirement, 9 yr 2 mo in), a median low point of $905k against $674k, and a worst ending of $1.09M against $835k, at the cost of a lower median ending, $1.81M against $2.10M. Against the plain index at 50/50 there was no such cost: it led on all four measures (
chapter 12

), with $755k against $662k at the worst low point, $905k against $771k at the median low point, $1.09M against $991k at the worst ending and $1.81M against $1.63M at the median ending. Set against the same two funds held at a fixed 70/30 or 50/50 and simulated as the rule is, without a Treasury-bill account, each of these comparisons goes the same way (
chapter 12
). The result has its limits: no fees, taxes or trading costs and no Treasury-bill account; settings declared in advance and never varied.
The hard stop over the long history.

Month by month from 1872, its median ending was close to a fixed 50/50's only over twenty and twenty-five years, and its floor depended on the withdrawal rule. Over twenty years its worst low point was above a fixed 50/50's under the study's rule; with withdrawals rising with inflation it was $232k (the 1903 retirement, 19 yr 11 mo in), below that of every fixed mix of stocks and bonds, from 70/30 to 50/50 — a fixed 50/50's was $490k. That $232k is the hard stop's, not picking once's twenty-five-year low point above, which happens to round to the same sum. From thirty years on the hard stop ran out more often than every fixed mix under both withdrawal rules, though over fifty years under the study's rule only narrowly: in 36 of 102, against 35 for a fixed 50/50.
Saving before retirement (Part IX).

The standard saver puts in $10,000 at the end of the first year and 3% more each year after. On the yearly history from 1928, saving into stocks alone was worth at worst 45.8% of the deposits made so far (the saver begun in 1928, in December 1931, 3 yr 11 mo in; at 70/30 60.4%, 60/40 65.7%, 50/50 71.2%), and month by month 36.6% (begun 1927, in June 1932, 5 yr 5 mo in); yet on the yearly history over twenty years it earned a median of 11.36% a year on the deposits, against 4.04% in bonds alone and 3.55% in cash alone, and over forty years even the worst stocks-alone saver earned 9.29% a year. Three principles apply throughout:
Every table and chart is generated, not transcribed.
They are produced directly from the backtest results, and the figures quoted in the text are drawn from the same results.
From the point each is introduced, every results table on the study's own years carries two benchmarks

chapter 6

chapter 8

and

, whose fixed mixes are the plain index's own two funds;
chapter 33

Every result is accompanied by its limitations.
A backtest of thirty years in a single fund family is evidence, not a forecast.
Nothing in this book constitutes investment advice.
How to read this book

Why does a book about choosing funds begin with cash? Because each piece of a retirement portfolio is judged against the simpler one before it, the book builds the portfolio one piece at a time, from the safest money to the choice of individual funds.
Part I, the question:
the retiree and the withdrawal rule.
Part II, safe money:
cash, then bonds from short to long term — what each does to a retirement on its own.
Part III, the S&P 500:
what the index is, a century of its history, and what holding it for decades has paid.
Part IV, mixing stocks and bonds:
why a mix works, the plain index (two Vanguard index funds) that serves as the yardstick, whether to restore the mix every year (chapters
to
), and then three chapters on the long market histories:
chapter 10

chapter 11

chapter 12

, a walk-forward rule that moves the split each January, and to 20% stocks and 80% bonds whenever the S&P 500 is 20% below its high, set beside the fixed splits; it closes with every retirement that ran out in the three chapters and what the markets did around them.
Part V, choosing funds — the method:
the funds a retiree could actually buy at each date, the prices, the ranking rule, the simulation and its assumptions, and the checks.
Part VI, choosing funds — the results,
in this order:
picked once and kept: the top funds chosen at retirement and never changed;
the list frozen at retirement: the funds offered on the first day of retirement, re-ranked within that list each January;
the menu rebuilt every year, the study's principal method;
the 1999 list, as a comparison;
followed by rebalancing frequency, five individual retirements and how long the money lasts.
Part VII, spending the money:
the bucket-of-money strategy (

and records the errors corrected during the study.

to
); it keeps two earlier savers for comparison (
chapter 35
) and closes with what it shows and does not (
chapter 36
The appendices
contain the glossary, the register of tests, the sources, the reproduction procedure, superseded analyses, every fund's quarterly and annual returns, and, in
appendix G

Readers new to investing should start at Part I. Readers who know the basics can start at Part IV, and readers with time for a single chapter should read
chapter 20
: what a retiree from 1995 onwards could actually have achieved with the funds available each year.

In Parts I to IV

thick lines are the fund-selection methods, the thin solid line is the plain index, and the pink line is SPY.

Terms used throughout:
The top two / three / four
— the two (three, four) best-ranked stock funds plus as many of the best-ranked bond funds, in equal amounts within the stock part and within the bond part.

— the split between stock funds and bond funds: 70/30 is 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds. All three were run for every method; most tables show 70/30 as the worked example, and the other two appear wherever they change the comparison. The bond part is always invested in bond funds, never held as cash; the only cash is the Treasury-bill account that holds the coming year's spending (
chapter 1
Complete retirement
— in the fund study, a 20- or 25-year retirement whose end lies inside the data (20 years: starts 1995-2006; 25 years: starts 1995-2001). Chapters
and

Ending balance / what was left

content.text: The Retiree's Portfolio
, chapters 1 and 2 of 36 —

The answer in brief
Part I: The question

Part I sets the terms: the retiree and the withdrawal rule that every portfolio in the book must carry. The chapters that follow put the same test to one portfolio after another — cash, bonds, the stock market, a mix of the two, and funds chosen by ranking: whether it can carry that rule, and how low it falls on the way.
Chapter 1. The retiree and the rule
What, exactly, must every portfolio in this book pay? This chapter fixes the retiree and the withdrawal rule that every simulation follows: an income that rises every year and is never cut.
The starting capital
The retiree invests

at the close of the first trading day of the year retirement begins (1 January is always a market holiday). Spending for the first year is assumed to be provided for separately, so the full amount is invested.
The withdrawals
At the end of the first year the retiree withdraws
4% of the initial capital, $40,000
. Each subsequent withdrawal is
3% larger than the one before
, regardless of market conditions. The amount is never reduced.

attrs.alt: Table: year; withdrawal — rows: 1, 11, 21, 30

content.text: Over a 20-year retirement the withdrawals total $1.07M, more than the original capital.

Does a 3% rise keep pace with prices? It is fixed; it is not an adjustment for inflation, and it does not change with what prices do. Consumer prices rose about 2.5% a year on average from 1995 to 2025, each year measured from December to December, so over the period as a whole the income rose a little faster than prices, though prices rose faster than 3% in 8 of 31 years. Every dollar figure in the book is in nominal dollars; chapters
and
also give returns after inflation.
Where the spending money is held
Each withdrawal passes through a
Treasury-bill account
before it is spent:
At the last close of the year
, the withdrawal is realised and transferred to the account.
Each month
, one twelfth is paid to the retiree.
While it is held
, the balance earns the 3-month Treasury yield.
At the next year end
, any interest remaining reduces the sale made at that year end.
The capital invested in funds is therefore always capital not yet required for spending.

attrs.alt: Figure 1.1: The withdrawal schedule: $40,000 at the end of year 1, rising 3% a year thereafter (bars), and the cumulative amount withdrawn (line).

content.text: Figure 1.1. The withdrawal schedule: $40,000 at the end of year 1, rising 3% a year thereafter (bars), and the cumulative amount withdrawn (line). The thick amber line is the cumulative total, read on the right-hand scale; the bars are each year's withdrawal, read on the left.
Rebalancing

The portfolio is rebalanced each January. The stock allocation is divided equally among the selected stock funds and the bond allocation equally among the selected bond funds, restoring the target allocation — for example 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds. The study ran every method at three splits, 70/30, 60/40 and 50/50; 70/30 is the worked example used through most of the book, and the others are reported beside it where they differ.
Rebalancing sells what has risen and buys what has fallen.
Chapter 9
asks whether to rebalance at all, and
chapter 22
examines rebalancing every six or every three months instead.
A worked example
A worked example (selected years) is set out in
appendix G.1

. It follows a retirement beginning in January 2000 with the two highest-ranked stock funds and the two highest-ranked bond funds on the list of that day — the 1999 list, which for a 2000 retiree is also the list frozen at retirement (chapters
and

; both are defined under "Terms used throughout" in "How to read this book") — re-ranked within it every January. It illustrates the mechanics only; the study's principal method, the menu rebuilt every year, is the subject of chapter 20. For each year shown, the worked example gives:
the amount due;
the interest left in the Treasury-bill account at the year end, which reduces the sale;
the amount sold;
the balance remaining.
Where should the $1M be held to pay that income? Part II begins with the answer that looks safest: cash, whose value never falls.
Part II: Safe money

Before stocks, the safest places a retiree can keep money: cash, then bonds. Part II follows the $1M, and the rising income it must pay, when none of it is ever exposed to the stock market. The result is the floor against which everything later is measured.
History, not a forecast.
These chapters show how cash and bonds behaved for retirements begun from 1995, under the interest rates of those years; they say nothing about the rates or returns to come.
Chapter 2. Cash

Cash never falls in value. Can it pay an income that rises every year, for twenty years and beyond? For a retiree drawing that income, the choice that looks safest is the riskiest of all: it runs out.
What cash means here

"Cash" is three-month United States Treasury bills, among the shortest and safest loans a saver can make. A money-market fund holds much the same thing. Here the cash account simply earns the Treasury-bill rate of the day, with no fees — a generous version of cash.
The rate has moved a long way:

From 2009 to 2015
it averaged 0.08% — for seven years cash earned almost nothing.
From 2016 to 2019
it rose again, to yearly averages between 0.3% and 2.1%.
it fell back to almost nothing: yearly averages of 0.04% to 0.36%.

A retirement held in cash
The same retiree as in chapter 1 — $1M, $40,000 in the first year, 3% more every year — with everything in cash, and in the safest bond funds (
chapter 3

The median after twenty years was

left of the $1M — the average of the 6th and 7th of the 12 endings, $156k and $222k, so no single retiree had it — and even the worst still held $120k. In the cash row the lowest value at any point is the ending itself, at the median and at the worst: the balance was at its lowest when the twenty years ended. Every cash retirement lasted the twenty years. The failure came after them:
Every retirement begun from 1995 to 2004 and held in cash then ran out of money
— the earliest start, the 1995 retiree in 2021, its 27th year; the latest, the 2004 retiree in 2025, its 22nd year.
No retirement held in a bond fund had run out by 9 October 2026.
But 4 held in Short-Term Treasury, those begun 1996 to 1999, held less on that date than the withdrawal due at the end of 2026: the 1996 retiree had $13k left against $97k due.
Why cash fails

The first withdrawal is 4% of the starting capital, and each one is 3% larger than the last. The Treasury-bill rate averaged below 4% in 20 of the 31 years from 1995 to 2025, and almost nothing from 2009 to 2015. Once the withdrawals exceeded the interest, the capital shrank, and the shrinking capital earned even less.

The lesson is not that cash is dangerous in a crash. It is that a fixed, rising income needs the capital to grow, and cash does not grow fast enough. Does lending for longer, at a higher rate, close the gap?

Chapter 3. Bonds, from short to long

A bond is a loan with a fixed term, and the longer the term, the more it usually pays. What does the extra pay cost? This chapter walks along the term — from bonds that mature in a year or two to bonds that mature in twenty or thirty — and sets what the extra years paid beside what they risked.
The trade-off
Short-term bonds
pay a little more than cash and barely move when interest rates change.
Intermediate-term bonds
pay more and move more.
Long-term bonds
pay the most, and their prices swing hardest: when rates rise their prices fall, and when rates fall their prices rise.

Vanguard offers each step in two kinds: Treasury bonds, backed by the United States government, and investment-grade bonds, lent to companies with good credit for a little more interest. At the short end there is a third, Short-Term Federal, which lends mainly to United States government agencies. Its prospectuses of 1999 to 2002 said that most of those bonds were not backed by the full faith and credit of the government, and those of 2003 and 2004 that many were not. Part III: The S&P 500

Before asking what stocks can do for a retiree, Part III asks what "the stock market" is. It introduces the market through its best-known index — what it is, how it has behaved over a century, and what holding it for ten to fifty years has paid.
History, not a forecast.
A century of returns is a record of what happened, decade by decade; it is not a guide to what the S&P 500 will return over the next ten, twenty or fifty years.
Chapter 4. What the S&P 500 is

"The market" usually means the S&P 500. Is it simply the 500 largest American companies? This chapter explains what the index actually holds, who decides what goes in, and why a handful of companies can steer it.
From 233 stocks to 500
the Standard Statistics Company built its first stock index: 233 U.S. companies, calculated weekly.
it became a 90-stock composite, calculated daily.
4 March 1957:
the S&P 500 was launched — 425 industrial companies, 25 railroads and 50 utilities, weighted by market value and, thanks to an early electronic calculator, computed every hour.

Index values before 1957 are reconstructed: the series runs back to January 1928, scaled so that its 1941-43 average equals 10. Chapter 5's history before 1957 is therefore the history of the earlier, smaller composite.

Today the index is run by S&P Dow Jones Indices, formed in 2012. On 30 September 2026 it held 503 stocks — more than 500 because a few companies are in it with two classes of shares — worth US$68.4 trillion together, about 80% of the value of U.S. shares available to the public.
Who decides what goes in

The index is not simply "the 500 largest companies". Membership is decided by an Index Committee of S&P Dow Jones Indices staff, which meets monthly and keeps its discussions confidential. It chooses among the companies that meet the published rules, "taking sector representation into account".
To be added today, a company must be:
American:
domiciled in the U.S., filing U.S. annual and quarterly reports, listed on a major U.S. exchange.
Large:

worth at least US$22.7 billion (since July 2025). The bar moves with the market — it was $5.0 billion in 2007, cut to $3.0 billion in the 2008 crisis, raised step by step since, and cut once more after the 2022 fall.
Widely held and traded:
enough shares in public hands and enough trading in them.
Profitable:
positive earnings in the latest quarter and over the last four quarters combined.
Seasoned:
a new listing must trade for at least twelve months first.

The rules apply to joining, not to staying: a member that later fails them is removed only when the committee judges that conditions warrant it. Changes are made as needed rather than on a schedule — from 1995 to mid-2021 there were 715 additions and 711 deletions, about 27 of each a year.
Weighted by size

Each company counts in proportion to its market value — its share price times the shares available to the public. Since 2005 only the shares that actually trade count; blocks held by founders, executives or governments are left out. S&P announced that change in March 2004 and phased it in over eighteen months.

Weighting by size means the largest companies dominate. In June 2024 the average member was worth US$96 billion, but the weighted average — the size of company a dollar in the index is actually invested in — was nearly US$1 trillion.
A handful of companies can steer it
How much of the index rides on its ten largest holdings, and has that share held steady? The share they held, a company's share classes counted separately:

content.text: S&P Dow Jones Indices reports that by mid-2025 the ten largest made up almost 40% of the index, "a level of concentration not seen since the mid-1960s". In June 1965 the ten largest — led by AT&T, General Motors and Standard Oil of New Jersey — held about 38%, adding up the weights in S&P Dow Jones Indices' table (the same article's text says "almost half"). Sixty years later those ten held a quarter of a percent each on average, and three had been through bankruptcy. None of the 2025 leaders was in the index in 1965.
The sectors move
What the index holds has changed with the economy:

attrs.alt: Table: year end; the five largest companies — rows: 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, February 2025

content.text: Energy in 1980:
three of the five largest companies — Exxon, Standard Oil (Indiana) and Schlumberger — were energy companies.
Technology in 2000:
information technology was 33.6% of the index in August 2000, at the height of the dot-com boom — and 33.0% again in March 2026.
Financial companies in the 2000s:
they reached a record 22.4% of the index in September 2006, according to Morningstar, shortly before the 2008 crisis.

The sector labels themselves have changed: the standard classification began in 1999, real estate was separated from financials in 2016, and in 2018 several internet and media companies moved into a widened Communication Services sector.
Dividends
The index's headline figure counts price changes only. Dividends matter far more than that suggests. By S&P Dow Jones Indices' calculation:
About 31% of the average monthly total return

from 1926 to February 2025 came from dividends — about half in the 1940s (53%) and the 1970s (50%), as little as 14% in the 1990s, and about 68% of the average monthly return in the 2000s, a decade whose total return, compounded, was negative (chapter 5).
Compounded, the gap is far larger:
from 1 January 1930 to February 2025 the index grew to 278 times its starting level on price alone, and to 9,584 times with dividends reinvested — about 34 times as much.
Every return in this book includes dividends, reinvested, unless it is marked "price only".
What this means for a retiree

Owning "the market" through the S&P 500 means owning what the committee admits, in proportions set by market value. That has worked well over long periods, but it is not neutral: when a few companies or one sector grow large, the index's path follows theirs — energy around 1980, technology in 2000, and the largest technology companies again today.
How has an index built this way rewarded those who held it, through crashes, inflation and booms? Chapter 5 follows it year by year from 1928, and decade by decade from 1930.
Chapter 5. A century of the S&P 500

A long-run average says little about the decade a retiree actually lives through. How different were the decades, and how deep were the falls between them? This chapter walks through them, using annual total returns — price change plus reinvested dividends — since 1928.
Decade by decade
The S&P 500 column gives the return in dollars, the last column what was left after rising prices. In which decade did stocks gain in dollars and still lose to inflation — and in which the reverse?

content.text: The 1930s:

the Depression. The table starts in 1930, so the boom of 1928 and the crash of 1929 are not in it. In dollars stocks returned -0.9% a year; consumer prices fell faster (inflation -2.0% a year), so after inflation stocks returned +1.1% a year. 10-year Treasuries, at +4.0% a year, did better than stocks.
The 1950s:
the best decade in the table, and the decade in which the 500-stock index itself was launched.
The 1970s:
stocks rose in name, but inflation took all of it and more — the column on the right shows what was left after rising prices.
The 1980s and 1990s:
two strong decades in a row, with falling inflation and falling interest rates.
The 2000s:
the "lost decade", two crashes in ten years, ending with less than it began.
The 2010s and 2020s:
recovery, and a long run of strong returns.
The worst and the best years

Since 1928 the S&P 500 lost money in 26 of 98 calendar years. The five worst were 1931 (-44%), 2008 (-37%), 1937 (-35%), 1974 (-26%), 1930 (-25%); the three best were 1954 (+53%), 1933 (+50%), 1935 (+47%).

The great falls

The worst years above were parts of longer falls. Which matters more to a retiree drawing an income: how far a fall went, or how long the wait for the recovery lasted? First the depth, measured from peak to trough:

the S&P 500 regained its peak on 9 July 1976, with dividends.
on 15 May 1989, with dividends — less than two years.
on 23 October 2006, with dividends.
on 2 April 2012, with dividends.
on 18 August 2020, six months after the peak, price only.
no new record close for 513 trading days, until 19 January 2024, price only.
For a retiree drawing an income, the length of the wait matters as much as the depth of the fall.

measures every stretch of ten to fifty years since 1928, and whether the falls were made up over the twenty or thirty years a retirement lasts.

Chapter 6. Holding the S&P 500 for decades

A retiree does not live through one year but through twenty or thirty. Does holding the S&P 500 that long remove its risk? This chapter looks at every stretch of 10 to 50 years since 1928, and then at the retirements this book follows. Its figures are before inflation unless stated.
Every stretch since 1928

Part IV: Mixing stocks and bonds

Parts II and III held cash, bonds and stocks each alone. Stocks left the most at the median, but with falls that are hard to live through while drawing an income. How much of that median can a retiree keep while softening the falls? Part IV puts stocks and bonds together. Chapter 7 shows why a mix works. Chapter 8 builds the plain two-fund mix that serves as this book's yardstick and sets it beside stocks alone and bonds alone.
Chapter 9
asks whether the mix should be restored every year.
Chapter 10
follows the same retirement rule over a century of yearly market history, from 1928, for the plain mixes that can be followed that far back;
chapter 11
follows it over a monthly history from 1872, and over retirements of forty and fifty years.
Chapter 12
tests whether a rule that moves the split as the market moves did better than a fixed split.
History, not a forecast.

The long histories show how these mixes behaved over twenty to fifty years in the past — through the crash of 1929 and the inflation of 1965-1982 among other times — not how they will behave. A rule that would have helped in those years is a description of those years, not a prediction.
Chapter 7. Why a mix

What does a retiree give up by holding bonds beside stocks, and what does it buy? Over ten and twenty years, with nothing withdrawn, a mix of stocks and bonds gave up some of the stock market's best outcomes to avoid most of its worst. Over longer periods, with nothing withdrawn, it simply earned less; with withdrawals, over twenty to thirty years, the worst retirement fared better with it, by its lowest point or by how many ran out (
chapter 11
follows retirements of forty and fifty years, where that edge was gone). This chapter measures the trade over a century.

earned far less at the median and at best over every horizon. Only their worst ten years beat the S&P 500's worst, which lost money.
More bonds moved the trade further.

At 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds, and at 50/50, the worst ten years earned 1.8% and 2.4% a year (1.1% at 70/30), the worst thirty years 6.6% and 6.1% (7.0%), and the median was lower over every length in the table.

The return a year over every 20-year period since 1928, by the year it began: the S&P 500 alone (pink), 70% S&P 500 with 30% 10-year Treasuries restored every year (the thickest line), 10-year Treasuries alone and 3-month Treasury bills; before inflation, nothing withdrawn. The mix ran below the S&P 500 for most start years. It ran above it in 10 of 79 periods, those beginning in 1928-1930, 1989-1990, 1992-1993 and 1998-2000: the earliest ran through the Depression, the later ones into the falls of 2000-2009. The thin grey line marks zero.
Why the mix helps a retiree in particular
A retiree sells every year to pay the income. In this book each withdrawal is taken from every fund in proportion to what it holds, so stocks and bonds are sold alike. The mix differs in two ways:
The balance falls less in a stock-market fall,
so each withdrawal taken near the low is a smaller share of what is left, and fewer stock shares are sold cheaply.
The split is restored each January.

After a fall in stocks the bond part is above its share and the stock part below it, so restoring the split sells bonds and buys stocks after they have fallen; after a strong year for stocks it does the reverse. It does not simply help: in the study's own retirements the yearly reset raised the worst ending but lowered the worst low point, at every split (
chapter 9
Does the same hold for real funds, priced daily and net of their costs, in the retirements this book follows? Chapter 8 builds the simplest such mix and sets it beside the S&P 500 alone.
Chapter 8. The plain index

What could a retiree have had without choosing any fund at all? The plain index is the simplest mix a retiree could hold, and the yardstick for everything that follows. This chapter defines it and shows how it fared beside the S&P 500 alone and beside the bond funds of
chapter 3
, each held alone.
What it holds
The plain index consists of two Vanguard index funds, held at a fixed split and restored to that split each January:
500 Index (VFIAX)
for stocks — a Vanguard fund that tracks the S&P 500 of Part III;
Total Bond Market Index (VBTLX)
for bonds — the fund of
chapter 3
that holds bonds of every kind and term in one.
At 70/30 it holds 70% VFIAX and 30% VBTLX. Before 2004 the older share classes of the same funds (VFINX, VBMFX) are used, because the early price records of the Admiral classes are unreliable (
chapter 14
). It represents the passive alternative: the outcome available without choosing any fund.

The plain index holds Vanguard's 500 Index fund, not SPY, the exchange-traded fund the book uses for its all-stock comparison. The two track the same index and ended close together: held alone, the 500 Index fund left a median of $2.46M and a worst of $397k over the retirements below, against $2.42M and $385k for SPY.
How it fared
Over the 12 complete 20-year retirements (start years 1995-2006), with 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds (
chapter 9
gives the plain index at 60/40 and 50/50 as well), what did SPY's higher median cost at the worst moment? The two low-point columns answer it:

and its worst ending more than twice SPY's: the 2000 retiree, the worst retirement for both, was protected by the bonds.
The price was the median:
SPY's was higher; stocks earned more over these twenty-year stretches.
Over twenty-five years the gap was wider still.

Only the 7 retirements begun 1995-2001 have run that long. At 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds, the plain index's worst ending was $892k and SPY's $244k, both for the retiree of 2000; the medians were $1.70M and $1.80M — lower than the twelve-start medians above because these seven start years include the hardest ones, 1999-2001. Long-Term Investment-Grade ended ahead of the plain index in 5 of 12 retirements

Long-Term Treasury did the same in 4 of 12

For the 2000 retiree, 6 of the 9 bond funds held alone ended ahead of the plain index's $835k
— every one except the three short-term funds. Beyond the two long funds, Total Bond Market left $1.08M, GNMA $1.08M, Intermediate-Term Treasury $1.21M and Intermediate-Term Investment-Grade $1.41M.

The price of holding a bond fund alone was the median: every one left less than the plain index, $1.78M for the best, Long-Term Investment-Grade (just ahead of Long-Term Treasury's $1.77M), against $2.10M.
Two things set apart the start years in which the long bond funds led:
The stock share.

With 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, the plain index met the stock-market falls of 2000-2002 early in these retirements and the fall of 2008-2009 midway, and each year's withdrawal was sold from a fallen balance. The bond funds held alone fell far less in both.
Falling interest rates
, which lifted the prices of long bonds most. These retirements ended by 2021, before rates rose in 2022.
Two yardsticks
Every method later in the book is compared with both SPY and the plain index. Neither is simply the harder one to beat:
SPY has the lower worst ending and low point, and the higher median
($2.42M against $2.10M). Against SPY, any portfolio holding bonds will generally fall less in a severe decline and earn less in a long rise, so the comparison mostly measures the stock / bond split.
The plain index is the like-for-like test.
It holds the same stock/bond proportions as the methods, so beating it requires the choice of funds itself to add value. It is the harder yardstick on the worst retirement.
The plain index is restored to its split every January. Is that trading worth doing, or would a retiree who bought the two funds once and left them alone have fared as well?

title: 9. To rebalance or not
subtitle: Restoring the split every January, or letting it drift: which kept the higher floor, and why the study rebalances

content.text: The Retiree's Portfolio

contents
— previous:
7–8. Why a mix, and the plain index
Chapter 9. To rebalance or not

Once a year the plain index is restored to its split: after a good year for stocks some are sold and bonds bought, after a bad year the reverse. What would change if the retiree never traded at all? This chapter asks what happens if the retiree does nothing instead, and simply lets the split drift while the withdrawals are taken from every fund in proportion.
The two choices
Rebalanced each January:
the split goes back to 70/30 (or 60/40, 50/50) at the first close of every year.
Left to drift:
the funds are bought once; nothing is ever traded again except the withdrawals, which come out of both funds in proportion to what each holds.
What happened
The table pairs each split rebalanced each January with the same split left to drift. Within each pair, does drifting move the worst ending and the worst lowest value the same way?

attrs.alt: Table: 20 years, retirements 1995-2006; median ending; worst ending; lowest value at any point: median; lowest value at any point: worst; biggest fall, withdrawals included, worst — rows: SPY, and others

content.text: It does not. At every split, leaving the mix to drift gave a higher lowest value at any point, at worst and at the median, but a lower worst ending: the two measures went opposite ways. Which matters more, the worst moment or the worst ending?

By the measure this book puts first, the floor, drift did better at every split. Its worst low point, at every split drifting or rebalanced the 2000 retirement's on 9 March 2009 (9 yr 2 mo in), was $544k against $492k rebalanced at 70/30, $635k against $573k at 60/40 and $727k against $662k at 50/50, and its median low point was higher too ($681k against $674k at 70/30, $729k against $721k at 60/40, $778k against $771k at 50/50). The cost was the worst ending, lower at every split: $762k against $835k at 70/30, $841k against $932k at 60/40 and $866k against $991k at 50/50.

Paired by start year, the drifting portfolio ended with more in 4 of 12 retirements at 70/30, 4 of 12 at 60/40 and 4 of 12 at 50/50 — in each case those that began in 2003-2006. Drift raised the stock share by the end of every retirement, and most in these, the only ones that began after the 2000-02 fall: their stock share drifted up through the long rise after 2009 and, at 70/30, the split had drifted to between 89/11 and 91/9 by the end of their twenty years, against the 70/30 restored each January. The higher drifting median at 50/50 in the table comes from those same start years, not from a general advantage.

content.text: Figure 9.1. What was left after 20 years, by year retired: the plain index at 70/30 rebalanced each January, the same two funds bought once and left to drift (withdrawals taken from both in proportion), and SPY. Line key: blue is the plain index rebalanced each January, cyan the same funds left to drift, pink SPY; each point is one retiree who started with $1M, marked by the thin grey line.
Why the two measures disagree
At 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds:
For the retirements that began in 1999-2002,

the drifting portfolio held fewer stocks after the 2000-02 fall and again late in the 2008-09 fall, because nothing was bought back: its split had drifted to between 54/46 and 63/37 at the start of 2003, and to between 50/50 and 60/40 at the start of 2009, against the 70/30 restored each January. Its low point, on 9 March 2009, was higher in every one of them — for the 2000 retiree, the worst retirement, $544k against $492k.
For those that began in 1995-1998,

it went the other way, and not for a single reason. The drifting portfolio's low point was the same for 1995 and 1996, which reached it in the first days of the retirement, and lower for 1997 and 1998; its biggest fall was larger for all four. No stocks were sold during the rise of the late 1990s, so all four met the 2000-02 fall with more in stocks: their split had drifted to between 77/23 and 85/15 by 1 September 2000, against 70/30 rebalanced.

the drifting portfolio regained its 2000 high, but went into the 2008 fall at 81/19, against 72/28 rebalanced, at the peak of 9 October 2007. Its biggest fall, from that peak to 9 March 2009, was 46.4% against 42.8%.
the drifting portfolio never regained its high of 1 September 2000 before the 2008 fall, so its biggest fall ran from that day to 9 March 2009 (1997: 46.8% against 44.3%).

ahead of the rebalanced portfolio on 1 September 2000, the drifting portfolios began 2003 behind it and with fewer stocks (67/33 and 63/37, against the 70/30 restored), stayed behind through the rise to 2007 and the fall that followed, and reached lower low points (1997: $931k against $968k rebalanced, on 9 March 2009).
Rebalancing buys stocks after a fall,
which deepens the next fall but takes part in the recovery; at 70/30 the rebalanced portfolio ended with more in 8 of 12 retirements.

Start year by start year, the drifting low point was not always the higher one. It was higher in 7 of 12 retirements at 70/30, 7 of 12 at 60/40 and 7 of 12 at 50/50. It was the same for 1995 and 1996 at 70/30 and 60/40, and for 1995, 1996 and 1997 at 50/50: each of these reached its low point in the first days of the retirement, before the two portfolios could differ. It was lower for 1997, 1998 and 2003 at 70/30 and 60/40, and for 1998 and 2003 at 50/50. At 70/30 each of these met a fall after a rise, with more in stocks than the rebalanced portfolio: 1997 and 1998 the fall that began on 1 September 2000, and 2003, begun after that fall, the fall of 2008-09, which its drifting portfolio entered at 78/22 at the peak of 9 October 2007, against 72/28 rebalanced.

The worst low point of every split, drifting or rebalanced, was set in March 2009, so none of them measures a deep fall late in a drifting retirement, when its stock share is highest. The retirements begun 2003-2006, whose drifting split rose highest, did meet two shorter falls late. At 70/30 they entered the fall of 2020 at between 82/18 and 86/14 (at the high of 19 February 2020) and that of 2022 at between 87/13 and 89/11 (at the start of the year), and fell 28.0% to 29.1% and 23.2% to 23.5%, against 24.2% and 21.6% rebalanced; their lowest values in those two years stayed well above their low points of March 2009.

Over these twelve retirements, then, the floor favoured drift at every split. The book nevertheless keeps rebalancing each January as its rule for every portfolio unless a chapter says otherwise, for a reason this floor does not measure: left alone, the split does not stay where the retiree set it. By the end of its twenty years the drifting 70/30 portfolio held between 74/26 and 91/9, depending on the start year, and the drifting 50/50 between 56/44 and 81/19: in all 12 retirements, more in stocks than the split chosen. Its higher floor came from the order of the falls: the hardest retirements, begun 1999-2002, had drifted toward bonds in the 2000-02 fall and met the 2008-09 fall with fewer stocks. Chapters
and
repeat this comparison for the chosen funds, and
chapter 22
rebalances more often than once a year.
These are retirements of one stretch of market history.
Chapter 10
takes the same rule back over a century, to the crash of 1929 and the inflation of the 1970s, which the study's retirees never met.

9. To rebalance or not
Chapter 10. A century of retirements

How would the plain mixes have fared for a retiree who began just before the crash of 1929, or at the start of the long inflation of the mid-1960s? The study's own retirements begin in 1995, and only 12 of them have yet run twenty years, so they cannot say. This chapter applies the same retirement rule to the yearly market history of chapters
to
chapter 11

applies it to a monthly history that reaches further back), for the plain mixes of stocks and bonds that can be built from them, and so follows 79 complete twenty-year retirements in the yearly data, begun every year from 1928 to 2006, instead of 12.
What is tested
The rule is the study's own (
chapter 1
$1M at the start of the first year,
divided between stocks and bonds;
$40,000 withdrawn at the end of the first year,
each later withdrawal 3% larger than the one before, never cut;
the split restored each January.

Each withdrawal is taken at the year end from the whole portfolio, stocks and bonds in proportion. Six portfolios are followed: the S&P 500 alone; 70% stocks and 30% bonds; 60/40; 50/50; a 10-year Treasury bond alone; and 3-month Treasury bills alone. Each is followed for 20, 25, 30, 40 and 50 years from every start year the data allow: 79 twenty-year retirements (begun 1928-2006), 74 of twenty-five years (begun to 2001), 69 of thirty years (begun to 1996), 59 of forty (begun to 1986) and 49 of fifty (begun to 1976).

The rule is also run a second way, with each withdrawal rising by that year's inflation (the change in consumer prices from December to December) instead of by 3%. Over this history inflation was far from steady: consumer prices fell 24% from 1930 to 1932 and rose 7.0% a year from 1966 to 1981. The two rules differ most in those years.

The long histories reach the start years the study cannot. At 70/30 under the study's rule, the three hardest twenty-year retirements began in 1928, 1929 and 1930, just before and during the crash; with withdrawals rising with inflation, the two hardest thirty-year retirements began in 1965 and 1966.
The data, and what they are not
Two long histories are used, here and in chapters
and
, both listed in appendix C:
the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested, a 10-year Treasury bond, 3-month Treasury bills and consumer-price inflation — the series of chapters
to
Monthly, January 1871 to August 2023:

the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested, built from monthly-average prices, a 10-year Treasury bond built from its yield, and a consumer price index (the file's own heading; it does not document how the index was compiled for its early years, appendix C).
Chapter 11
's retirements use its complete years, 1872-2022;
chapter 12
's rule reads it from January 1871. It has no Treasury-bill series, so no cash portfolio.
What they are not:
The bonds are a 10-year Treasury, not Total Bond Market.
A government bond of a single term behaves differently from a fund holding bonds of every kind and term, and nothing in this chapter says how Total Bond Market would have fared before it existed.
There are no fees
and no trading costs. The funds in the rest of the book are priced net of their costs.
There is no Treasury-bill account.
The study holds each withdrawal in Treasury bills for the year it is spent (
chapter 1
); here it is simply taken out at the year end, and the interest the account would earn is ignored.
Low points are seen only at year ends
in the yearly data, and only as monthly averages in the monthly data, so the lowest values read higher than they were: a fall and recovery within a year does not show.
Only the plain mixes go back this far.
Choosing funds needs the funds' own prices, which begin decades later.
Neither benchmark covers these years.

SPY's prices begin in 1993, and those of Total Bond Market, the plain index's bond fund, in December 1986: decades after the first start years here. The results tables below therefore carry neither SPY nor the plain index; the check that follows compares them over the study's own retirements, which both cover, and
chapter 12
follows the plain index's two funds day by day from December 1986.
Checked against the study's retirements

Before the long histories stand in for real funds, they are checked against them. Over the 12 retirements both cover — twenty years, begun 1995-2006, withdrawals rising 3% a year — each long-history row sits below the row of real funds it imitates:

content.text: Stocks alone tracked SPY.

In 10 of the 12 retirements the yearly S&P 500 ended between 1.8% below and 5.8% above SPY; for those begun in 2000 and 2001 it ended 9.1% and 10.1% lower. The yearly data measure each year from one year end to the next; the study's retirements begin at the first close of the year and follow daily prices.
The long-history 70/30 ended above the plain index in every one of the 12,

by between 2.3% and 16.1% (median 7.9%). It differs in its bonds (a 10-year Treasury instead of Total Bond Market) and in its costs (none); this chapter has not measured how much of the gap each explains.
These long-history mixes flatter:
over the retirements both cover, a retiree holding the plain index's funds ended with less.
Their low points read higher.
The worst low points in the yearly data lie above SPY's and the plain index's, which are read from daily closes: year-end values miss the bottom of March 2009.
Withdrawals rising 3% a year
In the "ran out" column, from which length of retirement did every mix reach zero at least once?

The lowest value at any point is read at year ends. The worst start was 1929, for stocks alone and for every mix, at every length.

At 70% stocks and 30% bonds it ran out in 1948, its twentieth and last year; the retirement begun in 1930 was left $143k after twenty years. Stocks alone ran out twice in twenty years, for the retirements of 1929 (in 1942) and 1930 (in 1944).
Over twenty years more in bonds raised the floor, and the median paid for it.

The two low-point columns show the floor first. At 70/30 the worst retirement ran out (1 of 79 retirements); at 60/40 the lowest value of any retirement was $105k and at 50/50 $228k, all three the retirement of 1929, while the median low point rose only from $976k to $987k. Bonds alone and cash alone ran down.

Their medians were the lowest at every length, and the longer the retirement the more often they ran out. Bonds alone never ran out within twenty years, but did in 21 of 74 retirements of twenty-five years and 32 of 69 of thirty; cash alone ran out in 8 of 79, 28 of 74 and 35 of 69 retirements of 20, 25 and 30 years. Over twenty years cash alone ended 53 of 79 retirements at its lowest value, and bonds alone 40 of 79: the withdrawals had outgrown what they earned.
Withdrawals rising with inflation
Does the same start year stay the worst when the withdrawals follow prices instead of rising 3% a year? The worst-ending column names the start year:

With withdrawals rising with inflation, the 1929 retirement no longer ran out within twenty years, in any mix or in stocks alone. Prices fell 24% from 1930 to 1932, and the withdrawal fell with them: $30k at the end of 1932, against $44k under the 3% rule. At 70/30 that retirement was left $531k after twenty years; its low point, $419k, came at the end of 1932, 3 yr 11 mo in. Over twenty years 1929 was still the worst start for stocks alone, 70/30 and 60/40; for 50/50 it was already 1965, which left $672k. Over 25 and 30 years stocks alone still ran out for the retirements of 1929 and 1930.
Over 25 and 30 years the worst starts were 1965 and 1966,

at the start of what the Federal Reserve's history calls the Great Inflation (1965-1982), for 60/40 and 50/50 at both lengths and for 70/30 at thirty years. Inflation averaged 7.0% a year from 1966 to 1981, and the 1966 retiree's withdrawal had reached $114k by the end of 1981, against $62k under the 3% rule. Over thirty years 70/30 was left $101k (the 1966 retirement); 60/40 ran out once (1966) and 50/50 twice (1965 and 1966).
Over twenty-five and thirty years more in bonds made the worst start worse, not better.
The 10-year Treasury earned 3.6% a year from 1966 to 1981, less than inflation, while the withdrawals kept pace with prices.
Over thirty years, bonds alone and cash alone ran out more often
than under the 3% rule: in 41 of 69 and 50 of 69 retirements, against 32 of 69 and 35 of 69.

Were

Month by month, from 1872

The monthly data check the yearly results and reach further back: 132 twenty-year retirements, begun 1872-2003, and the twenty-five- and thirty-year retirements beside them. Do the century's hardest starts look the same when the market is read twelve times a year?

content.text: Month by month the low points are lower; the medians agree.

Over the 76 twenty-year start years both cover (1928-2003), 70/30 under the 3% rule had a median low point of $949k in the monthly data against $992k in the yearly: twelve values a year catch more of each fall. Its median ending was $3.49M in the monthly data and $3.50M in the yearly.
One retirement shows how much lower.

With withdrawals rising with inflation, the 1929 retirement at 70/30 fell to $368k in June 1932 (3 yr 5 mo in), below the $419k its year-end values show; monthly averages themselves smooth the bottoms of falls.
At the worst they part.

The 1929 retirement at 70/30 ran out in its last year in the yearly data, and ended with $145k in the monthly data, where none of the 132 ran out (stocks alone: 2 of 132). A retirement at the edge can fall either side of it, depending on how the data are measured.
The worst starts mostly agree.

Under the 3% rule the worst start for every mix is 1929, at twenty, twenty-five and thirty years, in both data sets; with withdrawals rising with inflation both name the mid-1960s over thirty years. Over twenty-five years with withdrawals rising with inflation the monthly data's worst ending came from a start the yearly data cannot reach, the retirement of 1910, which left $650k at 70/30 and $639k at 60/40. It was not a lower ending than the yearly data's worst at 70/30 ($619k, the retirement of 1929), and the monthly 70/30's worst low point over those twenty-five years was still the 1929 retirement's: $368k in June 1932 (3 yr 5 mo in).
Forty and fifty years
The yearly tables of

From 70/30 to 60/40 to 50/50, at forty and fifty years, in both data sets and under both withdrawal rules, the number that ran out never fell, and 50/50 ran out more often than 70/30 in every case but one (yearly data, forty years, 3% rule: three each). With withdrawals rising with inflation, the mid-1960s starts failed again.
Over forty years in the yearly data 70/30 ran out in 3 of 59, 60/40 in 6 of 59 and 50/50 in 8 of 59; every 70/30 and 60/40 retirement that ran out began between 1962 and 1969.

ends with every retirement that ran out in chapters
to

What the long histories show, and what they do not
They show:
The hardest retirements of the century were harder than any of the study's twelve.
At 70/30 under the study's rule the plain index's worst twenty-year ending was $835k (
chapter 8
); over the century one such retirement ran out (the 1929 retirement, in the yearly data; in the monthly data none did).
The split mattered most at the worst, and which way depended on what went wrong.

In the deflation of the 1930s more in bonds helped: at twenty years under the 3% rule, in the yearly data, 70/30 ran out once and 50/50 never did. In the inflation of 1966-1981 more in bonds hurt: at thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation 70/30 never ran out and 50/50 did twice.
Over twenty years, stocks alone was never the better choice at the worst:
its worst low point and its worst ending were at or below 70/30's under both withdrawal rules, in both data sets.
Over forty and fifty years more in bonds did not protect:
as the bond share rose from 30% to 50%, the number of retirements that ran out never fell.
They do not show:
Anything about choosing funds.
Only the plain mixes can be followed this far back.
How Total Bond Market would have behaved.

The bond here is a single 10-year Treasury, and over the retirements both cover the long-history 70/30 ended above the plain index every time: in all 12 in the yearly data and in all 9 in the monthly (begun 1995-2003).
The future.
A century holds only a few retirements that began before a crash or a long inflation, and they are not independent: each twenty-year retirement shares nineteen of its years with the next one.
Exact endings or low points for a real portfolio.
With no fees the endings read high, and with low points read at year ends or as monthly averages the falls read shallower than daily prices would show.
More in bonds helped at the worst in the 1930s and hurt in the 1970s. A split that moves with the market might keep the first without the second.

title: 12, part 1. Moving the split: the rule, day by day
subtitle: A split that follows the S&P 500's recent lead, with a hard stop after a 20% fall, on the study's own index funds

content.text: The Retiree's Portfolio
, chapter 12 of 36, part 1 of 3 —
contents
— previous:
11. A longer history, and longer retirements
Chapter 12. Moving the split: a walk-forward rule
Chapters
and

held the split fixed for the whole retirement. Their hardest retirements began just before a long fall in stocks or a long inflation, and which split fared better at the worst depended on which of the two came. Can a rule that moves the split as the market moves raise the floor in both? This chapter tests one, and sets it beside the fixed splits on the same monthly history from 1872 and on the study's own two index funds, day by day, from 1987.
Why move the split

A fixed split holds the same share in stocks through every fall. A retiree at 70/30 in 1929 was restored to 70% in stocks and 30% in bonds each January while the S&P 500 lost 81.8% of its value, with withdrawals still due every year. The aim of a moving split is protection: less in stocks while a fall is under way, more while stocks lead.
The rule tested here is
walk-forward
: every decision is taken only from what had already happened by the day it was taken, and is carried out at the next month's (or the next day's) price, never at a price the rule has already read.

Its settings — the 20% fall, the one- and three-year comparisons, the splits — were declared in advance by the author from a reading of market history, not found by trying many values and keeping the best. Each version was run once, and every version run is reported here: the rule with two defensive splits, and its first version with the same two. Because they were chosen by someone who knows how past falls unfolded, the settings are not free of hindsight; what they are free of is tuning on these results.
The rule
50/50 at first:

the rule needs three years of history before it can compare, and compares only at the January check. It held 50/50 through 1989 in the daily data, which begin on 11 December 1986, and through 1874 in the monthly data, which begin in January 1871.
Each January, by the S&P 500's lead over bonds:

the S&P 500's total return over the past year and over the past three years is compared with that of bonds over the same periods. Ahead on both: 70% stocks, 30% bonds. Ahead on one: 60/40. Ahead on neither: 40/60.
A hard stop:

the moment the S&P 500 is 20% or more below its highest level so far (since the data begin), the portfolio moves to 20% stocks and 80% bonds, whatever the January comparison says. It stays at 20/80 until a January check finds the S&P 500 less than 20% below its high; from then the January rule applies again. The hard stop applies from the first day, the 50/50 years included.
Timing:
a decision taken on one month's (or day's) data is traded at the next month's (or day's) price. Between decisions the split drifts with the markets; each January it is restored.
Everything else is
chapter 10

's retirement: $1M at the start, $40,000 withdrawn at the end of the first year, each later withdrawal 3% larger (or changed by that year's inflation), taken from the whole portfolio at the year end; no fees and no Treasury-bill account.
Three other versions are run beside it:
The hard stop to 40/60:
the same rule with 40% stocks and 60% bonds as the defensive split.
The first version, to 20/80 and to 40/60:
it came back from the defensive split as soon as the S&P 500 led bonds over either one or three years, and could switch again only once the S&P 500 was back within 20% of its high.

The exit is what separates them. Day by day the first version switched 18 times, at both defensive splits, and 12 of those switches lasted 10 trading days or less: the S&P 500 was 20% below its high but still ahead of bonds over one year or three (over one year only in 4 of them), so the rule came straight back. On 29 August 2001 it came back with the S&P 500 23.6% below its high, and since it could not switch again until the S&P 500 had recovered to within 20% of that high, it never returned to its defensive split through the fall that followed, to 47.5% below the high on 9 October 2002: the version to 20/80 held 60/40 for the rest of 2001 and, by the January rule, 40/60 through 2002 and 2003. The hard stop held 20/80 from March 2001 until the January check after 2004.
The data, and the checks
Monthly, January 1871 to August 2023:
the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested and a 10-year Treasury bond —
chapter 11
's monthly data, built from monthly-average prices. The rule reads them from January 1871; the retirements begin in 1872, as in
chapter 11
, which uses the complete years 1872-2022. The S&P 500's high and its falls are read from those averages.
Daily, 11 December 1986 to 9 October 2026:
the study's 500 Index fund and Total Bond Market fund, from their dividend-adjusted closing prices; here the 500 Index fund stands for the S&P 500, and Total Bond Market for bonds.
The fixed splits are run the same way as the rule,
bought at the January price rather than at the end of the December before, so their monthly figures differ from
chapter 11

's: a little at the median, a lot at the floor. Over twenty years under the 3% rule their medians are 1.2% to 4.1% lower (70/30: $2.03M against $2.05M), and both name 1929 as the worst start, but that retirement's ending was $45k here against $145k in
chapter 11

at 70/30, $191k against $275k at 60/40 and $311k against $380k at 50/50. The month's difference also moves a retirement at the edge from one side to the other, so the counts of retirements that ran out differ too: over thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation the fixed 70/30 ran out in 0 of 122 retirements in
chapter 11
and in 1 of 122 here, the retirement of 1966.
Neither benchmark reaches back to the monthly data:
SPY's prices begin in 1993 and the study's retirements in 1995. Over the retirements both cover, the study's own twelve, the second daily table below sets them beside the rule.
Checked against the study's retirements:

for every one of the 12 retirements begun 1995-2006, the daily fixed 70/30 ended 0.5% to 2.0% below the study's plain index — the same two funds, without the Treasury-bill account in which the study's retirees hold the coming year's spending, and whose interest they earn.
As in
chapter 10
, there are no fees, taxes or trading costs. The rule trades more often than a fixed split, at every switch and every January, and in a taxable account each trade could realise a gain.
Twenty years, day by day
In this table every row's worst low point is the 2000 retirement, in March 2009 (9 yr 2 mo in), so the fifth column compares like with like: which portfolio held the most at that moment?

$755k, against $489k for a fixed 70/30 and $658k for a fixed 50/50, every one the 2000 retirement in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in. Its median low point ($946k, against $917k and $937k) and its worst ending ($1.09M, against $819k and $976k) were above both as well. Here the floor came without a cost against a fixed 70/30: the median, $2.50M, lay between the fixed 70/30's $2.42M and stocks alone's $3.00M.
The hard stop to 40/60
had a worst low point of $645k (also March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), below the fixed 50/50's, and a median of $2.41M.
The first version had the lower floor at both defensive splits:
worst low points of $707k (to 20/80) and $636k (to 40/60), against the hard stop's $755k and $645k, all four in March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in. Its medians were higher: $2.88M and $2.69M.
Over the study's own twelve retirements, beside the two benchmarks:

Every worst low point here is the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009 (9 yr 2 mo in). Against the plain index at 50% in stocks and 50% in bonds (
chapter 9

it led on all four measures, with a worst low point of $755k against $662k, a median low point of $905k against $771k, a worst ending of $1.09M against $991k and a median ending of $1.81M against $1.63M. The hard stop to 40/60 led on three: its median low point ($806k), worst ending ($1.01M) and median ending ($1.85M) were above the plain index's, but its worst low point, $645k, was below it.
Twenty retirements that overlap by up to nineteen years are one stretch of market history, not twenty separate ones.
Day by day, with withdrawals rising with inflation, and over longer retirements
Does the daily order hold when each withdrawal rises with inflation instead of 3% a year? Over the same twenty-year retirements:

attrs.alt: Table: daily, 20 years: 20 retirements, and others

content.text: The hard stop to 20/80 again had the highest worst low point:

$765k, against $666k for a fixed 50/50, $496k for a fixed 70/30 and $717k for the first version to 20/80, every one the 2000 retirement in March 2009 (9 yr 2 mo in). Its median, $2.61M, lay between the fixed 70/30's $2.53M and stocks alone's $3.12M. On the daily data the rule kept the highest floor under either withdrawal rule; on the monthly data, with withdrawals rising with inflation, it did not (the section "Twenty years, month by month").
Over twenty-five and thirty years fewer daily retirements are complete: 15, begun 1987-2001, and 10, begun 1987-1996.

attrs.alt: Table: daily data (median ending / worst ending; lowest value at any point, and others

content.text: Over twenty-five years

the worst low points of the mixes and the rule are still the 2000 retirement's, in March 2009 (9 yr 2 mo in), and the hard stop to 20/80's was the highest of every row under both withdrawal rules: $755k under the 3% rule, against $658k for a fixed 50/50, and $765k with withdrawals rising with inflation, against $666k.
Over thirty years

the retirements end with those begun in 1996, and every worst low point is the 1990 retirement's, in October 1990 (0 yr 9 mo in). There the fixed 50/50 and 60/40 held more ($936k and $918k under the 3% rule) than the hard stop to 20/80, which held the January rule's 70/30 through 1990 and fell to the fixed 70/30's $899k.
No daily retirement ran out,

Twenty years, month by month, from 1872

Month by month the rule can be followed over 132 twenty-year retirements, begun 1872-2003. Whether its floor still led depended on how the withdrawals grew. First the study's rule, withdrawals rising 3% a year:

content.text: The hard stop to 20/80 had the highest worst low point in the table:

Then the same retirements with each withdrawal rising with inflation. Which column shows whether the rule kept its promise of protection? The worst lowest value: read the hard stop's row against the fixed mixes'.

Begun in 1903, with the same withdrawals, the fixed mixes and stocks alone ended between $813k and $1.01M, against the hard stop's $232k (under the 3% rule, between $903k and $1.10M, against $329k). fell to $461k (the 1903 retirement, December 1922, 19 yr 11 mo in): above the fixed 70/30 and 60/40, below the fixed 50/50.

Twenty-five and thirty years

Over twenty-five and thirty years more of the retirements reach zero, so the floor and the count of those that ran out carry the comparison. Where the hard stop ran out and a fixed 50/50 did not.

Start year by start year

Did the rule's protection come from many retirements or from a few? When the hard stop was on
Day by day, the hard stop switched 6 times:

What the rule shows, and what it does not
Is the rule protection, then? It shows:
A higher floor where the withdrawals rose 3% a year.

Day by day, over the retirements begun 1987-2006, the hard stop to 20/80 had the highest worst low point of every portfolio, with a median between a fixed 70/30's and stocks alone's; over the study's own twelve its worst low point was $755k against the plain index's $492k (both March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in), for a lower median ending. Month by month under the 3% rule it had the highest worst low point over twenty and twenty-five years.
Day by day, a higher floor with withdrawals rising with inflation too,

over twenty and twenty-five years: over twenty its worst low point was $765k, against $666k for a fixed 50/50 (both the 2000 retirement, March 2009, 9 yr 2 mo in). Over thirty years, which only 10 daily retirements have run, the fixed 50/50 and 60/40 held more.
Month by month, a lower floor where the withdrawals rose with inflation.

Over twenty years its worst low point, $232k (the 1903 retirement, December 1922, 19 yr 11 mo in), was below every fixed mix's (from $348k for 70/30 to $490k for 50/50, each the 1929 retirement, June 1932, 3 yr 5 mo in), and over twenty-five years it ran out once where no fixed mix did. Like the fixed splits of chapters
and
, it protected against some histories and not others.
Month by month, close to a fixed 50/50 at the median over twenty and twenty-five years, not beyond.

At those lengths the 20/80 version's median ending was within a tenth of a fixed 50/50's under both withdrawal rules (over twenty years under the 3% rule, $1.70M against $1.67M); from thirty years on it differed by more, and over forty and fifty years it was 31% and 71% above under the 3% rule and 12% and 25% below with withdrawals rising with inflation. At the floor the withdrawal rule decided: under the 3% rule it was slightly above a fixed 50/50 over twenty years and well above over twenty-five; with withdrawals rising with inflation it was far below over twenty years, and over twenty-five it ran out where the 50/50 did not.
It did worse where the retirement was long.

Over thirty years with withdrawals rising with inflation both versions ran out more often than every fixed split; over forty years under the 3% rule, more often than every fixed mix; over fifty, the 20/80 version still did.
It does not support:
That a moving split beats a fixed split in general.
On the long history it did not; the daily result covers one stretch of twenty overlapping retirements.
That these settings are the best ones.
No other values of the fall or the comparison periods were tried, and no defensive splits beyond the two shown; other values would give other results.
Anything net of costs.
There are no fees, taxes or trading costs, and the rule trades more than a fixed split.
The future.
The history holds only a few deep falls, and the next need not resemble them.
Every retirement that ran out
Chapters

to 12 give, for every portfolio, length and withdrawal rule, how many retirements ran out. Which ones were they, and what did the markets do around them? Appendix G.13 lists every complete one, with the year of the retirement in which it ran out, and beside them the 105 retirements still under way, all cash alone or bonds alone in the yearly data, that have already run out. None ran out in the daily data, under any version of the rule or any fixed split.
Every retirement holding stocks that ran out — stocks alone, a fixed mix or the rule — began in one of four stretches of years. Bonds alone and cash alone ran out far more widely:

content.text: A start year counts once for each portfolio, length and data set in which it ran out, so a single hard start can stand behind many of the results counted above. This chapter's fixed splits and stocks alone are counted beside
chapter 11
's monthly rows: they are the same portfolios on the same monthly data, bought a month later, and 188 of their 227 results repeat a
chapter 11
result for the same start year.
Begun 1872-1894: falling prices and withdrawals rising 3% a year
Only the monthly data reach these years.

All but 2 of the 306 results that ran out were under the 3% rule, over 30 years or more; the exceptions are the hard stop to 20/80's retirement of 1893, over forty and fifty years. They ran out between 1908 and 1942.
Prices fell while the withdrawals rose.

Consumer prices fell 48.5% from December 1872 to December 1896. The 3% rule raised the withdrawal regardless: by the end of 1896 the 1881 retiree was drawing $62k, where withdrawals rising with inflation would have been $26k. Under withdrawals rising with inflation, no retirement holding stocks that began before 1893 ran out, at any length.
Returns were modest.
From 1881 to 1920 the S&P 500 earned 5.5% a year and the 10-year Treasury 3.5%; forty years of the 3% rule need 5.4% a year if the return is the same every year.
No archived source used in this book names an event for these years,
so only the data are described.
Begun 1898-1911: the inflation of 1916-1920, then the crash of 1929
Monthly data only:

109 results under the 3% rule and 91 under withdrawals rising with inflation, over 25 to 50 years; they ran out between 1926 and 1960. 125 of the 200 are the rule's own: 75 for the hard stop and 50 for its first version.
Consumer prices rose 88.3% from December 1915 to December 1920.
From 1903 to 1920 the S&P 500 earned 4.6% a year, about the rate of inflation (4.6%), and the 10-year Treasury 3.3%, less.
The fall of 1929-1932 then came late in these retirements,

in years 19 to 32 of them, for all but 4 results: the hard stop to 20/80's retirement of 1903, with withdrawals rising with inflation, had already run out, in 1926, year 24, over each length of twenty-five years and more (the section "Twenty years, month by month" shows the rule's timing in it).
Begun 1928-1940: the crash of 1929 and the 1930s
Both data sets and both withdrawal rules:
143 results under the 3% rule and 38 under withdrawals rising with inflation, over 20 years and more; they ran out between 1942 and 1985, as early as year 14 of the retirement.
The S&P 500, dividends reinvested, fell 81.8% from September 1929 to June 1932

(monthly averages), and did not regain its September 1929 level until January 1945, 15 years later. Consumer prices fell 27.2% from September 1929 to March 1933, and from 1930 to 1940 the S&P 500 returned -0.9% a year and the 10-year Treasury 4.0%. Under the 3% rule the withdrawals kept rising through all of it.
The Federal Reserve's history of the crash

dates Black Monday to 28 October 1929, and records that the Dow Jones Industrial Average, price only, stood 89% below its peak by July 1932 and did not return to its pre-crash level until November 1954.
The retirements begun 1936-1940 ran out only over forty and fifty years, and late.

Those begun in 1936 and 1937 met a second fall early — the S&P 500's monthly averages fell 41.6% from March 1937 to April 1938, in the recession the Federal Reserve's history dates from May 1937 to June 1938 and calls the third-worst downturn of the twentieth century — and outlasted it. Those begun in 1939 and 1940 began after that low and met another fall within their first years: from the January they began to April 1942, the monthly averages fell 23.5% to 25.7%. Their 23 results ran out between 1975 and 1985, in years 39 to 49 of the retirement, 20 of them under withdrawals rising with inflation: they ran out during and after the inflation of the late 1960s and 1970s, described for the starts of 1959-1969 below, not in the fall of 1937-38. Across the whole group, 50 of the 181 results ran out in 1965 or later.
The hard stop held 20/80 through both:
for 85 months after its switch in 1929, to the check after December 1936, and for 79 months after 1937, to the check after December 1943.
Begun 1959-1969: the Great Inflation (1965-1982)
Every one under withdrawals rising with inflation:
232 results, over 25 to 50 years, in both data sets; no portfolio holding stocks begun in these years ran out under the 3% rule. They ran out between 1989 and 2012.
Inflation outran both stocks and bonds.

Consumer prices rose 7.0% a year from 1966 to 1981, while the S&P 500 earned 6.0% a year and the 10-year Treasury 3.6% (yearly data). The withdrawals rose with prices: the 1966 retiree's had reached $114k by the end of 1981 (
chapter 10
Within those years the S&P 500's monthly averages fell 39.2%
from January 1973 to December 1974, and were back at that level in July 1976.
The name
is the Federal Reserve's: its history of the period files the years 1965-1982 as the "Great Inflation".
Bonds alone and cash alone
Bonds alone ran out in 802 results and cash alone in 335,
across the start years in the table above.
The 10-year Treasury earned 2.7% a year from 1941 to 1981,

less than the 3% yearly rise of the withdrawals and less than inflation (4.7%); from 1982 to 2020 it earned 7.8%. Over forty years under the 3% rule, in the yearly data, which begin in 1928, every bonds-alone retirement begun from 1928 to 1963 ran out, and none begun later; in the monthly data, those begun 1872-1959 and 1961 ran out.
The order of the returns mattered as much as their average.

Bonds alone begun in 1955 earned 5.7% a year over its forty years, more than the 5.4% a steady return would need, and still ran out, in 1978, year 24 of the retirement: over those 24 years it had earned 3.1% a year.
Treasury bills earned 0.3% a year from 1933 to 1945:

under the 3% rule cash alone ran out within twenty years for every retirement begun from 1931 to 1938. They earned 0.5% a year from 2009 to 2021, and the forty-year cash retirements begun 1982-1986 ran out late, in years 33 to 40. Those begun 1987-2004, not yet forty years old, have already run out, sooner: in years 22 to 32.
Apart from the bond funds held alone in
chapter 8

, every portfolio in Part IV holds the market itself, through the indexes or two index funds. Could a retiree have done better by choosing funds, and how can a choice be tested without knowing, as no retiree could, which funds would do well?
