title: 13–15. The method: the funds, the prices, the selection rule
subtitle: Which Vanguard funds could be chosen each January, where the prices come from, and how the funds were ranked

content.text: The Retiree's Portfolio
, chapters 13 to 15 of 36 —
contents
— previous:
12, part 3. Moving the split: every start, and every run-out
Part V: Choosing funds — the method

A rule that picks past winners is easily made to look better than any retiree could have done: rank it on today's list of funds, which holds only the survivors, or let it buy at a price the ranking has already read. How did the study keep out such hindsight, and where could it not? This part sets out how each result is produced, in five steps: the fund universe, the prices, the selection rule, the simulation, and the checks applied to it.
Chapter 13. The fund universe

Which funds could a retiree of 1995 actually have chosen from? Not those on offer today, which are the ones that survived. This chapter defines which funds a retiree may choose from, and limits every choice to the funds that could actually be bought on that date. Without that limit, the results would carry decades of hindsight.
Which funds are eligible
Why Vanguard.
The study keeps to one fund family, and to Vanguard's, for three reasons:
Long records.
The oldest price records the study uses begin in 1980, so from the study's first year funds could be ranked on ten-year records (chapter 15).
No sales loads.

The fee tables of the archived prospectuses read "Sales Charge (Load) Imposed on Purchases: None", so the price is what an investor paid; a few funds charged a purchase or redemption fee at times, which the study does not model (
appendix G.2
lists them).
Low costs.
In 1999 the 500 Index fund's total annual operating expenses were 0.18% and Total Bond Market's 0.20%; these costs are already deducted from the prices the study uses (chapter 14).
One family keeps the menu, the share classes and the price records consistent; it also confines the evidence to that family (
chapter 27
The investable universe is restricted to Vanguard funds:

attrs.alt: Table: included; excluded — rows: Stock funds, Bond funds

content.text: Also excluded:
asset-allocation and LifeStrategy funds;
funds of funds;
ESG-screened and factor funds;
Core Bond, which may hold up to 10% in bonds outside US dollars;
Core-Plus Bond, by the author's choice (no archived filing of the fund gives a reason);
funds offered only to institutions.
Funds are held in their retail share classes:
the lower-cost Admiral class
where the fund offers one, from the first trading day of 2004, or from the Admiral class's first price if that came later;
an older class of the same fund
before that, normally the original Investor class;
the Investor class throughout
for the few funds that never offered Admiral shares, such as Dividend Growth and Selected Value.
Four funds depart from these rules (chapter 14):
Morgan Growth
offered Admiral shares from 14 May 2001, but the study uses its Investor class's published yearly returns throughout.
Long-Term Bond Index
is priced on its Admiral class alone, from 7 February 2019, because its Investor class's prices were not available.
Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index
are priced on their exchange-traded classes until their Admiral classes' first prices, although each also had an Investor class: the price records hold no Investor-class prices for either fund (
chapter 16
gives the effect):

Dividend Appreciation Index: an Investor class from 2006; priced on the exchange-traded class until December 2013, so the portfolios that held it from 2012 to December 2013 were valued at exchange-traded prices;

High Dividend Yield Index: an Investor class from 2006; priced on the exchange-traded class until February 2019, so the portfolios that held it from 2016 to February 2019 were valued at exchange-traded prices.
Funds that later merged or were liquidated are included until the year end before the event (
chapter 16
Only what was available on the day
The governing principle is that
a retiree may select only from funds that existed, and were open to new investors, on the date of selection.
A list of today's funds consists of survivors — funds that performed well enough to remain in existence. Applying it to a retiree of 1995 would confer 31 years of hindsight.

The fund menu was therefore reconstructed as it stood at each year end from 1994, fund by fund, from Vanguard's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. For each fund the menu records the date it was:
launched;
offered to retail investors;
closed to and reopened for new investment;
merged or liquidated.
Closures and reopenings are those found in the filings that were read. For the 1990s the evidence is thinner. It consists of:
the closures of Windsor, PRIMECAP and Trustees' Equity U.S., read in their own filings;
Vanguard's family-wide notices of funds not accepting new accounts, which name only Windsor and PRIMECAP — and no such notice was found for October 1996 to April 1998;
each other fund's prospectus of late 1998 or early 1999, which shows no closure, though the longer ones were read only in part.

Windsor's reopening on 1 June 1999 is inferred rather than read: its prospectus of February 1999 still shows it closed, and that of June 1999 no longer does. Any date between the two gives the same menus, because the menu changes only in January: Windsor could first be bought in January 2000 either way.
A missed closure of another fund in the 1990s therefore cannot be ruled out (
appendix G.2
Four ways to apply the menu
The menu is applied in four ways, each consistent with the date of selection:
the menu each January
chapter 20
) — the funds available each January from 1995, ranked afresh every year; this is the principal method;
the list frozen at retirement
chapter 19

) — the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement (for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994), frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January; a variant reviews the list every 3 or 5 years instead;
the 1999 list
chapter 21
) — the menu on 31 December 1999, kept throughout; applicable only to retirements beginning in 2000 or later, and presented as a comparison;
picked once and kept
chapter 18
) — the top funds on the menu on the first day of retirement, held for the whole retirement without re-ranking.
The table summarises the size of the menu and the highest-ranked funds at intervals. Which kind of bond fund fills the last column, and in which row does that change?

attrs.alt: Table: January; stock funds that could be picked; bond funds that could be picked; the top two stock funds; the top two bond funds — rows: 1995, 1998, 2000, 2003, 2006, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025

content.text: A long-term bond fund holds one of the top two bond places in every row shown up to 2020, and neither place in 2025. Across every January, not only the rows shown, a long-term fund held one of the two places from 1995 to 2022 except in 2004, and after that only in 2024; chapters
and
return to what that meant. The stock leaders change more often: twelve different funds fill the eighteen places, against seven in the bond column.
The number of funds that could be picked grew from 17 in January 1995 to 50 in January 2025, as new funds were launched. Closures, mergers and reopenings moved it in both directions along the way.
The full detail is set out in
appendix G.2
the complete year-by-year menu;
the menus at the 1994-1998 year ends as published by Vanguard;
the 1999 list fund by fund;
the closures and mergers used, with the sources for them.
When a fund closes or reopens
Three rules govern changes in availability:
Closed at a year end:
a fund closed to new investors cannot be purchased in the following January.
Closed while held:
a fund already held when it closes is retained until the next January and then sold.
Reopened:
a fund that reopens may be purchased again at a January rebalance if it ranks highly enough.
The portfolios picked once and kept (
chapter 18
) depart from the second rule by design. An existing holder keeps a fund that closes, and adds to it each January only as far as the fund's closure terms allowed.
Chapter 18
also applies this keep-a-closed-fund rule, as a variant, to the menu each January and the list frozen at retirement.
The menu settles which funds could be bought. What each of them then returned is a question for the price records.
Chapter 14. Prices and data

Can a database of fund prices be taken on trust? In this study it could not, and every result rests on the price records. This chapter describes where they come from, how they were checked against Vanguard's own published returns, and what that check corrected.
The source

Daily prices are taken from a database of dividend- and distribution-adjusted closing prices. These represent the value of a holding with every distribution reinvested on the date the price records carry it.
The records are used in three forms:
as extracted
, one series per share class;
one continuous series per fund
, built from them:
the Admiral share class from the first trading day of 2004 (the early Admiral records are unreliable), or from the Admiral class's first price if that came later, as for these funds:
June 2005: Inflation-Protected Securities;
September 2011: Small-Cap Growth Index, Small-Cap Value Index, Mid-Cap Growth Index and Mid-Cap Value Index;
December 2013: Dividend Appreciation Index;
February 2019: High Dividend Yield Index;
an older class of the same fund before that, normally the Investor class, but the exchange-traded class for Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index (chapter 13);
the Investor class throughout for funds that never offered Admiral shares, such as Dividend Growth and Selected Value;
the Admiral class alone for Long-Term Bond Index, from 7 February 2019, because its Investor class's prices were not available;
the same set extended
with the funds added to the menu after 1999.

Daily prices are missing for five funds that later merged into other funds. Each is represented by its published annual returns; two of them, Trustees' Equity U.S. and Morgan Growth, were on the menu in the 1990s.
These are Investor-class returns throughout. For Morgan Growth, the only one of the five any portfolio held (from 2000 to 2018,
chapter 16

), this is one of the departures from the share-class rule noted in chapter 13. Its Admiral shares date from 14 May 2001, so the share-class rule would have used them from 2004; the study uses its Investor class's published yearly returns instead.
From 2004 it was held by:
the top-four portfolios picked once at the 2000 and 2001 starts, from 2004 to 2018, at 17.5% of the funds' value at 70/30 (less at the other splits);
the top four of the lists frozen at retirement, at the same share: the list frozen at the 1995 retirement in 2016 and the lists frozen at the 1995 to 1998 retirements in 2018;
the top three of the list frozen at the 1995 retirement, at 23.3%, in 2018 alone.

The fund's own prospectuses put the Admiral class's expenses 0.14 to 0.19 percentage points a year below the Investor class's in fiscal years 2004 to 2008 (its 2009 prospectus) and 0.10 to 0.14 in 2014 to 2018 (its 2019 prospectus); the Admiral class's published return was 0.10 points higher in 2008 and 0.10 in 2018. On a 17.5% holding, the understatement is therefore roughly 0.02 to 0.03 points a year of the portfolio's return, and about 0.02 at 23.3% (2018, a gap of 0.10) — an approximation, not a measured figure.
The check against published returns
The prices were verified against Vanguard's published calendar-year returns for every fund from 1985 to 2003.
The verification proved material: the database omitted a substantial number of capital-gain distributions, principally through 1993 (
chapter 27
). Two corrections followed:
Each year that disagreed
with the published figure was restated to it.
The funds whose earliest years could not be verified
begin at the end of 1987 (U.S. Growth) or 1988.
Traceability
The study uses 291 price files across the three forms above:
284 of the funds' mutual-fund share classes (a series can appear in more than one form);
two: the exchange-traded classes of Dividend Appreciation Index and High Dividend Yield Index (chapter 13);

five others: SPY in each form; RSP, an exchange-traded fund extracted as a second benchmark and not used in this book; and the 3-month Treasury-bill rate. Behind the restated series are 31 untouched extracts. Each file is identified by a recorded checksum, so that the inputs to every result can be established exactly.
The share classes used in each period, every data correction and the cross-checks are documented in
appendix G.3
With the menu and the prices in place, one decision remains each January: which of the funds on the menu to hold.
Chapter 15. The selection rule

Does a fund that has led over the past five and ten years go on leading? The selection rule is a wager that it does, and Part VI tests the wager. The rule ranks funds on past return and holds the leaders. This chapter states it exactly.
Each January, separately for stock funds and for bond funds, every fund available that day is ranked using data up to the previous year's final close only:
History:
a fund requires
at least five years of history
to be ranked.
Ranking:
it is ranked on its
five-year return
and on its
ten-year return

, and the two ranks are averaged. A fund's rank is one plus the number of funds with a higher return. The ten-year rank is taken only among the funds that have ten years of history; a fund with less than ten years is ranked on its five-year return alone.
Example:
in January 1998 U.S. Growth was 10th of 13 on five years and 3rd of the 7 funds with ten years: a score of 6.5, the average of the two. The lowest score ranks first.
Ties
are resolved in favour of the higher five-year return.
Holdings:
the portfolio holds
the top two
stock funds and the top two bond funds (the top three or four in alternative versions), in equal amounts within each asset class.
Timing:

the ranking uses prices up to the last trading day of the old year (31 December, or the last trading day before it). Every purchase — the first one and each later change of holdings, together with the annual rebalance — is made at the close of the first trading day of the new year, so nothing is bought at a price the ranking has read.
The ranking considers return alone; it takes no account of risk, expenses or changes of management.
The table in chapter 13 shows the highest-ranked funds at intervals. Every January's selections at two, three and four funds, with the corresponding holdings of the 1999 list, are set out in
appendix G.4
Old funds ranked as if young

History is counted from the start of a fund's price records, not from its launch. Eight funds ranked in the mid-1990s have price records that begin only at the end of 1987 or 1988, because their earlier years could not be verified (chapter 14).

In the Januaries shown below, each had been running for ten years or more but had no ten-year return in its records, so it was ranked on its five-year return alone. In earlier Januaries a fund launched less than ten years before was genuinely young and is not counted. Did the shortened records reach what was bought? The last column shows when the menu each January picked these funds.

attrs.alt: Table: fund; launched; price record from the end of; Januaries ranked on five years alone, though ten years old; picked in those Januaries (the menu each January) — rows: Explorer, Windsor II, and others

content.text: Four of them were among the top two in at least one of those Januaries.

Windsor, whose records also start late, was closed to new investors in those years and was not ranked. The lists frozen at retirement and the portfolios picked once used the same scores. How the results would change if these funds had their full ten-year records has not been measured.
Three later funds were also ranked on a record shorter than their lives:
Growth Equity

joined the menu on 12 June 2000, carrying the record of Turner Growth Equity — but only from 1999, although Turner Growth Equity was launched in 1992. With less than five years of record it could not be ranked in the Januaries of 2001 to 2003. It was then ranked on its five-year return alone in 2004 to 2008: last in 2004 to 2007, and 8th of 22 in 2008. Whether its full record would have changed those Januaries, or let it be ranked in 2001 to 2003, has not been measured.
Dividend Growth

is counted only from 6 December 2002, when it became a diversified stock fund; its earlier record, as Utilities Income, a sector fund, is left out by the rules of chapter 13. It was therefore ranked on its five-year return alone in 2008 to 2012, and was one of the top two stock funds in 2009, 2010 and 2012 and third or fourth in 2011.
Long-Term Bond Index

, launched in 1994, has usable prices only from 7 February 2019 (chapter 14). It was ranked on its five-year return alone from its first January, 2025: 20th of 22 in 2025 and 2026 among the bond funds, so it was never picked.
The rule decides what is bought each January. How a retirement is then followed for twenty years or more, and by what it is judged, is the subject of

title: 16–17. The method: the simulation, the measures, the checks
subtitle: How each retirement is simulated, what every measure means, what the simulation assumes, and how it was checked

content.text: The Retiree's Portfolio
, chapters 16 and 17 of 36 —
contents
— previous:
13–15. The method: the funds, the prices, the selection rule
Chapter 16. The simulation and the measures

Twenty years or more of daily values have to be reduced to a few figures before two ways of choosing funds can be compared. Which figures, and in what order should they be read? This chapter describes how the study's own retirements are simulated, and defines every measure reported for them:
It covers the retirements begun from 1995 on the daily fund prices:
the fund-selection methods of Part VI, and the cash, the single funds, SPY and the plain index of Parts II to IV.
Chapters
to
and
state their own data and assumptions,
which differ from those below: chapters
and 28 each in a section of their own, and
chapter 10
's section covers
chapter 11
's monthly data too.
The simulation
The simulation follows one retirement at a time: a start year, a horizon of 20 or 25 years (or "to date", to the last available close), a portfolio, and the withdrawal rule of
chapter 1
. It walks every trading day and:
restores each fund to its target weight at the first close of each January — the only point at which stocks are traded against bonds (the variants of
chapter 22
also do so every six or three months);
takes the withdrawal at the last close of each year, from every fund in proportion to its value, so the withdrawal leaves the weights unchanged;
pays the T-bill account out monthly and accrues its interest.
It is run for every start year from 1995 to 2025 and for every portfolio; Part VI reports the results.
A
complete retirement

is one whose whole horizon lies inside the price records. Only complete retirements enter the median and the worst. With a 20-year horizon there are twelve of them, starting from 1995 to 2006 (seven for the 1999 list, which starts in 2000).
All figures for the simulated retirements are in nominal dollars, before taxes and before trading costs. The after-inflation figures of chapters
and
come from yearly index returns, not from this simulation.
The measures
Every measure reported for these retirements is defined once, here:

attrs.alt: Table: measure; meaning — rows: ending balance, lowest value at any point, biggest fall, time to recover, never back, longest underwater, ran out, ahead of the plain index, share of what was left, and others

content.text: Withdrawals are included in every measure. A portfolio that declines 40% while paying out $40,000 a year or more takes longer to recover than an index chart suggests. The time to recover reported here reflects that.

The median ending and the lowest point answer different questions. The median ending is what a typical retirement left behind. The lowest point is what the retiree had to live through, and the moment at which a retiree is most likely to abandon the plan or return to work. Wherever methods are compared, the book therefore reads the table above in this order:
the worst lowest value at any point
, with when it came;
the median lowest value;
the worst ending;
the median ending
, given as the cost of a higher floor, never as the verdict on its own.
Where the floor and the median point opposite ways, both are stated; "The ranking and the comparison" below gives a case.
What the simulation assumes
Every retirement this chapter covers rests on the assumptions below. Each is a choice, and a different choice could change the figures.
The retiree
Follows the rule mechanically
for twenty years or more: never sells in a fall, never changes the spending, and has no other assets or income in the model.
Holds the funds directly with Vanguard,
one account per fund, with no transaction fees.
Pays no tax.
Distributions are reinvested in full; switching gains, rebalancing gains and Treasury-bill interest are untaxed; withdrawals are gross.

The figures therefore describe a tax-deferred account such as an IRA, before tax on withdrawals and without required minimum distributions. In a taxable account the realised gains would be taxed. That cost falls mostly on the selection methods: a switch sells a whole holding, while the plain index's January rebalance sells only the excess. Tax on distributions falls on both.
The money
All simulated figures are in nominal dollars.
The withdrawal rises a fixed 3% a year, not with measured inflation. A balance that grows from $1M to $2M has not doubled in purchasing power.
The first year's spending is set aside on top of the $1M.
The retiree effectively starts with about $1.04M, and the first sale from the funds comes after a year of growth — gentler than the common 4% rule, which withdraws at the start.
The ending balance excludes the next year's spending,
already moved to the Treasury-bill account.
Withdrawals come from every fund in proportion,
not from bonds first or from a separate reserve. Only the January reset (and the in-year resets of
chapter 22
) trades stocks against bonds.
The Treasury-bill account

Chapter 17. Checks and reproducibility

How would anyone know if a figure in this book were wrong? A backtest can be wrong in ways that produce entirely plausible figures: a fund bought while it was closed, a purchase at a price the ranking had already read, a table left over from an earlier version of the method. This chapter lists the controls that guard against that.
The following controls are applied to every result of the fund-selection tests (
appendix B
Independent rebuilds.
For a few retirements per test, the portfolio's growth is recomputed from the raw prices by a separate, independent calculation. It must agree with the simulation to six digits.
Availability compliance.

Every holding in every year is checked against its closure periods, menu dates and merger or liquidation dates. A fund bought while it could not have been bought is an error. A fund is held while closed in two cases only:
it closed during a year in which it was held, and is kept until the next January (rule 2 of
chapter 13
) — under the menu each January, for example, PRIMECAP in 1998;
an existing holder keeps it on purpose (
chapter 18
); the January additions to it stay within its closure terms, but the in-year resets of
chapter 22
top it up without that limit (chapter 16). Across the tests, tens of thousands of yearly holdings were checked; none failed.
Unchanged means identical.

When the method changes, every result it should not affect is rerun and must come out exactly the same as before. For example, when new measures were added, every existing measure in every set of results had to come out unchanged.
Full reproduction.
Every test and every table was once regenerated from scratch and compared with the recorded results: nothing differed. After each correction described in
chapter 27
every test still in use was rerun, and each later test was checked against an independent rebuild.
The ends of every derived series.
The first and last values of any curve built for a chart or a table are printed and checked before anything is quoted from it.
Benchmarks in every comparison of the fund methods.
SPY and the plain index sit beside every table that compares the fund-selection methods. The long histories of chapters
to
and Part IX reach back before either benchmark existed; chapters
and
each say how they handle that.
The long histories were checked against the study's own retirements over the years both cover:
chapter 10
sets its mixes beside SPY and the plain index, and
chapter 12
compares its daily fixed 70/30 with the plain index.

Every figure taken from the results, the price records or the archived filings is computed when the book is assembled, and assembly stops if a sentence no longer matches the data. The other figures are the study's own settings (
chapter 1
) or dates and terms typed from the filings and research notes listed in
appendix C
, each with its source recorded. Independent reviews have recomputed the book's figures (
chapter 27

Not every test was declared in full before it was run. A group of earlier tests changed the holding method without declaring it; they were repeated with re-ranking every January, and every test from that repeat onwards was declared in full before it was launched. The earliest of the group were not repeated on their own: they differ from a repeated test only by its closure rule, and once funds are re-ranked every January that rule changes no holding, because a closed fund cannot rank among the open ones. Each test's method and results are recorded, so the exact method behind every result can be recovered;
appendix B
lists every test.

With the menu, the prices, the rule, the measures and the checks set out, the results can be read. The floor and the median ending can point opposite ways, and not the same way for every method. chapter 18

Part VI: Choosing funds — the results
Does choosing funds by their records do better than simply holding the plain index — at the worst moment on the way, at the end, or both?
History, not a forecast.

Every result in this part is the record of a few overlapping retirements begun from 1995 — 12 complete over twenty years, 7 over twenty-five. A method that did well in them is not shown to do well in future, the funds it held are named as history, not as picks, and no future selection is offered.
Every retirement in this part follows the same rules:
Starting capital:

Withdrawals:
$40,000 at the end of that year, rising 3% a year thereafter — $1.07M over twenty years.
Measure of outcome:
the capital remaining.
Amounts:
nominal dollars, before taxes and trading costs.
The chapters move from the simplest way of choosing funds to the most active:

(chapter 18) — the top funds chosen on the first day and kept, a fund being replaced only if it merges away.

Counts of retirements "ahead of the plain index" turn, in a few cases, on margins under 1% of the plain index's ending balance. With 70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds, 2003 is such a near-tie for 15 of the 45 methods reported in this part and appendix G (each number of funds, each way of restoring the mix and each closure rule counted separately), and 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998 or 1999 for a few others. At the other splits the near-ties fall mostly in other years: with 60% in stock funds and 40% in bond funds, 1997 for eight of the 33 methods reported; with 50% in each, only 1996 and 1998.
A count alone is therefore not a meaningful difference when it moves by one or two between methods. What matters is the margin behind each retirement that changes sides.
Chapter 18. Picked once and kept
The simplest approach of all is to choose once and keep the choice. Can the funds picked on the first day of retirement simply be held for twenty years?
A result that depends heavily on luck.

The method in this chapter produced the deepest worst low point and the lowest worst ending among the 70/30 portfolios, and also the highest median of any method in the study apart from two variants of itself (only the stock / bond split restored, $2.87M; a closed fund topped up without limit, $2.84M). All three come from a handful of decisions made once, on the first day of retirement. Whether those first picks happened to include a fund that would outperform for the next twenty years was not knowable from the ranking; the same rule, applied at the start of 2000, chose the two that fared worst over the twenty years that followed, of the 13 stock funds that could be picked that January (with nothing withdrawn: U.S. Growth 1.94 times its starting value, Growth Index 2.97 times; the other 11 between 3.15 and 5.26 times). The retiree of 1999 had chosen the same two, again the worst two of the 12 that could be picked that January. The figures below describe what happened to twelve retirements, not what the method can be expected to deliver.
The rule

On the first day of retirement the retiree buys the two (in a second version, four) highest-ranked stock funds and bond funds on that January's ranking. The retiree keeps them for the whole retirement, restoring the 70/30 allocation each January.
Two events can change a holding:
A fund closes to new investors:
it is kept, since a closure stops new accounts and an existing shareholder is never required to sell.
A fund merges away:
it is replaced by the fund it merged into, or, if that fund is already held, by the highest-ranked fund of the same type on that January's menu.

In practice only one merger touched a holding: Morgan Growth, merged into U.S. Growth on 5 April 2019, in the 2000 and 2001 retirements holding the top four. The merger was announced on 17 December 2018, so the replacement at the January 2019 ranking used only what a retiree could have known. No fund picked was liquidated.

Morgan Growth's prices are known only as calendar-year returns, so its moves inside a year are smoothed. For the top-four retirement that began in 2000 (70% in stock funds and 30% in bond funds), this hides part of the fall from its high in September 2000 to the 2009 low:
chapter 16

estimates its lowest value at $414k to $421k rather than $443k, and its biggest fall at 61.0% to 62.1% rather than 58.0%, which would make it the worst fall of the top four (estimates, not simulated results). The 2001 top-four retirement's low on 9 March 2009 is affected in the same direction (its 2007 high has not been examined); that effect has not been measured.
Buying more of a closed fund

Keeping a closed fund raises a second question. Restoring the allocation each January means buying more of any fund that lagged the rest of the portfolio in the year just ended. Whether an existing shareholder could still buy depended on the terms of each closure.
Vanguard's closure notices, filed with the SEC, set those terms out. The closures that affect these retirements:
PRIMECAP:
Capital Opportunity:
March 2004 to April 2013, and again from December 2013 (still closed).
Explorer:
For these closures an existing shareholder could add up to $25,000 a year. Reinvested dividends were exempt from the limit wherever a notice addresses them.
Dividend Growth (2016-2019), which some of the re-ranking retirements below keep, stayed open to existing shareholders without limit. Selling was never restricted.
The method is therefore measured three ways:
Limited:
the January purchase of a closed fund limited to $25,000 a year, as the notices provided. This is the version shown first.
Unlimited:
without any limit.
None:
with no purchase at all.

Whatever a closed fund cannot take goes to the open funds of the same kind — stock or bond — in proportion to their targets. When every stock fund held is closed, there is no open stock fund to take it: what cannot be bought stays in the bond funds, and the split is not fully restored that January. That needs both conditions at once — every stock fund closed, and one of them below its target by more than the $25,000 it may still take:
The 2002 retiree,

The 1995 retiree,
holding PRIMECAP and Explorer: both were closed in January 2007 and 2008, and money stayed in the bond funds only in January 2008.

Chapter 19. The list frozen at retirement
The method of
chapter 18

tied each retirement to its first choices. A middle course fixes the list of funds on the first day of retirement but re-ranks within it each January, so a fund that falls behind is replaced. Does freezing the list, instead of rebuilding it from the whole menu each January, change the outcome?
The principal method of the study, set out in full in
chapter 20
, is the menu each January: every January the retiree re-ranks all the funds Vanguard offers that day and holds the top two stock funds and the top two bond funds.

Against it, reviewing the list at intervals changes little, and where it moves the floor it lowers it. Retaining the list without review held less at its worst moment — less even than the plain index — but ended higher than the menu each January, at the median and in the worst ending. Is that a better result? The answer depends on which measure comes first.
How the list is compiled

An alternative to the menu each January is to compile the list once, at retirement, from the menu of that day — for a 1995 retiree, the menu at the end of 1994. The list is then either retained or reviewed at intervals.
Within the list the funds are still re-ranked each January and the top two of each type held.
The list frozen at retirement is the list retained: the funds Vanguard offered on the first day of retirement, frozen then — funds launched later never join — and re-ranked within it each January.
Reviewing every three or five years
Reviewing the list every three or five years held up no better than the menu each January at the worst moment, and in places worse:
Worst low point:
every three years $515k, the same as the menu's; every five years $506k, against $515k (each 9 yr 2 mo in).
Median low point:
every three years $748k, against the menu's $755k; every five years $755k, the same.
Worst ending:
every three years $692k, the same as the menu's; every five years $660k, against $692k.
Median ending:
$1.78M for all three.
Retirement by retirement, in every complete retirement but one, both reviews end the same as the menu each January or slightly lower:
Every three years:
six of the 12 retirements end lower, by up to $67k; six end the same; none ends higher.
Every five years:
eight end lower, by up to $58k; three end the same; one ends higher (2003, by $1,530).
Ahead of the plain index:
the list reviewed every 5 years in 3 of 12, against 2 of 12 for the menu each January and for the list reviewed every 3 years.

Chapter 20. The menu each January

Does re-picking the best-ranked Vanguard funds every January do better than simply holding the plain index? The method has been available to any retiree since 1995, and it is the principal result of the study. Which held up better in March 2009, the menu or the plain index — and which ended with more? The lowest-value and ending columns of the table below answer both, and they point in opposite directions.
How the menu is built
Each January the retiree:
reviews the funds Vanguard offers that day;
retains those with at least five years of history;
ranks them on their five- and ten-year records;
holds the two highest-ranked stock funds and the two highest-ranked bond funds.

The process is repeated every year. No information unavailable at the time is used, as far as the filings allow, with one exception: a fund that later merged or was liquidated leaves the menu at the year end before the event (
chapter 16

). Apart from that, every fund selected was open to investors on the date of selection. For the 1990s the closures come from the filings read for three funds (Windsor, PRIMECAP and Trustees' Equity), from Vanguard's family-wide notices — with none found for October 1996 to April 1998 — and from each other fund's late-1998 or early-1999 prospectus, the longer ones read only in part; a missed closure of another fund cannot be ruled out (
chapter 13
, appendix G.2).
The method needs no list fixed at any date. It applies identically to every start year from 1995.

Chapter 21. The 1999 list, from 2000

What if every retiree from 2000 onwards had used one list, Vanguard's menu at the end of 1999? Applied from 2000, the 1999 list ended ahead of the plain index in every one of its seven retirements. Was it the safer choice as well? At its worst moment it held less. This chapter sets out both, and explains why the list is presented only as a comparison.
The list
The 1999 list is a single list: Vanguard's menu at 31 December 1999, retained throughout and re-ranked within itself each January.

Only retirements beginning in 2000 or later could have used it. For earlier retirements it contains funds added to the menu after the retirement began. It therefore covers only 7 complete retirements, 2000 to 2006.
For the 2000 retiree it is identical to the list frozen at retirement, and produces exactly the same result.

Part VII: Spending the money

Parts II to VI asked what the retiree should hold. Every retirement in them drew its spending one year at a time, at the year end, and in the study's own retirements that year's spending was then held in Treasury bills while it was paid out. Part VII asks whether drawing the money differently would have helped, and in particular whether a larger reserve of cash, kept apart from the investments, would have carried the retiree through the worst years with more to spare.
History, not a forecast.

This part reruns the retirements of the earlier parts — the study's own, begun from 1995, the two index funds day by day from 1987, and the monthly market history from 1872 — under other ways of drawing the money. It reports what each way would have done in those years. It does not estimate what any of them will do in future, and it recommends none of them.
Chapter 25. The bucket-of-money strategy

Would two years of spending held in Treasury bills, apart from the stocks and bonds, have kept the retiree's money higher at its lowest point? With such a reserve the retiree never has to sell in a falling market to be paid. What does the reserve cost, and who bears that cost: the typical retiree, or the one who began at the worst moment?
One design, set down in advance

Bucket strategies take many forms. They differ in how many years of spending are held in cash, in when and from what the cash is refilled, in whether gains are moved into it, and in what happens to cash that is not needed. This chapter tests one design. Its rules were set down by the author before any result was seen, and nothing in them was tuned: each version was run once, on every portfolio of the earlier chapters, and every version run is reported here.
Version 1, the study's rule
chapter 1
), is itself a one-year bucket:
the year's withdrawal is sold at the last close of December, from every holding in proportion;
it is held in the Treasury-bill account and paid to the retiree in twelve monthly parts through the next year;
at the next close, the first of January, the mix is restored to its target.
Version 3, the two-year bucket
, keeps more in bills and fills it in two ways:
At the start,
two years of withdrawals — $81,200 under the 3% rule — go into Treasury bills, the bucket; the rest of the $1M is invested at the target split.
Every payment

comes from the bucket, on the dates and in the amounts of the study's Treasury-bill account — each year's withdrawal in twelve monthly parts — so in the study's retirements the retiree's income is identical in every version.
Each quarter,

at the last close, the invested money alone is checked. A side — the stocks or the bonds — more than 5 percentage points above its target share (above 75% in stocks at 70/30) is sold back to its target share at the next close, and the proceeds go into the bucket, not into the other side. This sale is called a trim below.
Each January,

at the first close, the bucket is topped up to the next two years' withdrawals, selling the overweight side first and then the other; then the invested money is restored to its target split. Anything in the bucket beyond two years' withdrawals stays there, in bills.
The bills earn

the 3-month Treasury rate: the daily rate from 1990; before it, Damodaran's yearly return on 3-month bills (appendix C), held flat within each year, from 1928; and nothing before 1928, where neither exists.
Version 3 with smaller trims

reads the trim differently: it sells only the amount by which the side exceeds its target share of the money invested before the sale. At 70/30 that is 30% of the full trim when the stocks are trimmed and 70% when the bonds are, and it leaves the side above its target until January restores the split. It is reported beside version 3 as the one variation run, not as a separate design. Two further versions, which change only when and from which side the year's withdrawal is taken, are the subject of the last section but one.

Where the portfolio holds funds, the stock side is the total of its stock funds and the bond side the total of its bond funds; a trim sells a side's funds in proportion, and the funds held still change only in January. SPY and stocks alone have no bonds and so no trims; the bucket and its January top-up apply to them as to every portfolio. The hard-stop rule of
chapter 12
uses the split in force at the check as its target, 20/80 while it is defensive.
The measures are those of
chapter 16

, with the bucket counted as part of the money. The lowest value at any point is the invested money plus the bucket, less the payments still owed in the current year; the ending leaves out the coming year's spending, as version 1's does; and a retirement ran out when a payment could not be made. In the daily and monthly data, version 1 is

takes it at December's last close from the overweight side first — the stocks or the bonds, whichever is further above its target — and from the other side only if that is not enough; the restoration follows at the next close, as in version 1.

Across all 73 such portfolios of the study and of the daily data — every method, number of funds and split, and both withdrawal rules — no measure moved by more than 2.6% over twenty years, or 3.7% over twenty-five.
The January restoration undoes the difference.
Whichever side the withdrawal is taken from, the restoration at the next close sets both sides back to their targets; what is left is one trading day's movement of the markets on the amount moved.
The single funds have no restoration to undo it.

SPY and stocks alone have no other side, so version 2.0b is version 1 exactly. Version 2.0a moves each year's sale one trading day later, and that moved SPY's worst ending from $385k to $411k, more than any measure of any mix moved.
What this chapter shows, and what it does not
It shows

that this two-year bucket raised the floor of the plain index and of the fixed mixes over twenty years, in the study's retirements and in the daily data from 1987 — the plain index's worst low point by 5% at 70/30 — at a cost of 15% of its median ending.
It shows

that the same design lowered the floor of every fund method, of SPY over twenty-five years, and of the fixed mixes in the monthly history from 1872 under both withdrawal rules, where it also ran out more often in the longer retirements.
It does not show

what any other bucket design would have done. The surplus never reinvested is a specific choice: a trim's proceeds stay in bills however large the bucket grows. A design that returned the surplus to the investments, refilled the bucket only after a rise, or held a different number of years was not tested. The one variation run, the smaller trims, cost less than the full trims for every portfolio holding bonds, and in some cases raised the floor above version 1's.
It does not show
that the order of the withdrawal is irrelevant for a portfolio without a January restoration: for the single funds it was not.
It is history, not a forecast.
The retirements here are the earlier chapters' own, a few overlapping stretches of the past; the bucket's results in them say how it would have behaved then, not how it will behave.

Chapter 27. Errors and known limitations

Why should any figure in this book be trusted? Not because none was ever wrong: a backtest that has never been found in error has usually not been examined closely. This one was in error several times, and in almost every case the error produced plausible figures.

What can be offered instead is the record. The errors are listed below by subject, with the date each was identified and its effect where it was measured, because the corrections form part of the result. Seven known limitations, not yet corrected, follow them, and the chapter ends with how the errors were found.
Errors of method
An undeclared change of holding method
(identified 11 October 2026)
What was wrong.

The method specified by the author re-ranks the funds every January. After one comparison favoured selecting the funds once and holding them throughout retirement, a series of tests used that alternative without declaring it.
Correction.
Every one of them still in use was repeated with annual re-ranking. The others had already been superseded for a different reason (
appendix E
Since then.
No method is adopted because it scored better, and every test declares its holding method. Picking once and keeping (
chapter 18
) is now studied as a declared method of its own.
Closed funds topped up without limit
(identified 12 October 2026)

Picking once and keeping restores each fund to its target every January, which can mean buying more of a fund closed to new investors. The first version allowed unlimited purchases. 27. Errors and known limitations
Part IX: Before retirement

Every retirement in this book began with $1M already saved. This part asks the question that comes first: what did the same markets and the same portfolios do for money being put in, year after year, before retirement? One standard saver is followed through the same records as the retirees — the yearly record from 1928, the monthly record from 1872, the study's two index funds day by day from 1987, and the fund methods from 1995 — and measured as the retiree was measured, the floor first.
Chapter 28 sets out the saver, the measures and the data.
Chapters 29 to
follow the saver through a century of yearly data, a century and a half of monthly data, and the index funds day by day.
Chapter 32
tries the hard stop of
chapter 12
on a saver, and
chapter 33
the fund methods of Part VI.
Chapter 34
asks how long it took to reach $1M, and what the last five years before retirement did to the account.
Chapter 35

Chapter 36
sets out what this part shows and what it does not.
History, not a forecast.
As before, these are past savers' accounts over ten to forty years, not an estimate of what saving will earn.
Chapter 28. The saver
The retiree of
chapter 1
withdraws $40,000 at the end of the first year and 3% more each year after. The saver of this part does the reverse:
The account starts empty.
$10,000 is deposited at the end of the first year, and each later deposit is 3% more than the one before: $13,048 in the tenth year, $17,535 in the twentieth, $31,670 in the fortieth.
Nothing is withdrawn.
Over ten years the deposits add up to $114,639; over twenty, $268,704; over thirty, $475,754; over forty, $754,013.
Each deposit is invested at the year's last price,

in the portfolio's holdings in their proportions of the day, and the portfolio is restored to its split each January — the same moments at which the retiree's withdrawal is sold and the retiree's portfolio restored. On
chapter 32
's monthly table, which follows the rule of
chapter 12
, the split is restored at the January price instead, as
chapter 12

A retiree's worst moment is the lowest value along the way. A saver's account starts at nothing, so its own lowest value is the empty account and says nothing about a loss. What does is whether the account was ever worth less than the money put into it, and by how much. Six measures follow each saver, in the order the book reads them:
The floor: the lowest value as a share of the deposits so far.

Each time the account is valued — each year end, month end or close, before that day's deposit — its value is divided by the money deposited up to then. The lowest such share is the saver's floor, given with its month and the time into the saving at which it came. Below 100%, the account was worth less than had been put in.
The largest shortfall:
the same comparison in dollars, the most by which the account fell short of the deposits made so far.
The annual return on the deposits:
the single yearly rate at which the deposits, each compounded from the year end it was made, would have grown to the ending.
The ending:
the account's value at the last year end, after the last deposit.
Reaching $1M:
whether, and when, the account first stood at $1M — the sum with which every retirement in this book began.
The last five years:

the largest fall from the account's highest value so far within the last five years of the saving, the fall met just before the money was to be used. Chapter 36. What this part shows, and what it does not
It shows, the floor first:
A saver's floor can lie far below what was put in.

Saving into stocks alone, the deepest floor was 45.8% of the deposits at year ends, 36.6% month by month, and 52.3% day by day on the study's index funds, where every twenty-year saver went below its deposits at some close.
Time changed the outcome for stocks.
Over ten years the worst stocks-alone saver lost money on every record; over forty years even the worst earned more than the median saver in bonds alone.
Among stocks alone and the three mixes, the more in stocks, the lower the worst return over twenty years or less,
and at every length the higher the median return and the sooner the $1M.
Over twenty and thirty years the hard stop of
chapter 12
raised the saver's floor and lowered the median return,
and month by month, over twenty years and more, its worst saver earned the least.
Choosing funds did not help the saver.
No fund method raised the floor above the plain index's, and most earned less at the median; SPY earned the most and fell the deepest.
The last five years could take a large part of the account:
for thirty-year savers in stocks alone, at worst 80.8% month by month in 1932, 36.7% at the year end of 2002 and 33.8% day by day in 2020.
It does not show:
What a saver should do.
How much to save, in what mix, and when to move from saving to spending are not answered here; nor is the choice of the 3% rise.
Anything net of taxes or inflation,
or, on the yearly and monthly data, of fees. Every dollar figure is nominal and before taxes; only the daily and fund-study figures are net of the funds' own costs.
The future.
The yearly record holds 59 forty-year savers, but only two forty-year spans that do not overlap; the monthly record, three. Each saver shares most of its years with its neighbours.
One life from saving to spending.
This part stops at the $1M with which the retiree of
chapter 1
begins; the book does not follow one person through both.

Every retirement in this book began with a sum already saved. The saving that came before it, in this record, was neither smooth nor certain over ten years; over twenty years and more, every saver on every record and in every portfolio ended with more than it had put in.
